item.title: Yankees At-Bat(s) of the Week: Anthony Volpe (9/10)
item.author: Peter Brody
item.content:encoded: I’m sure Anthony Volpe wanted to make a statement in his first game back from his demotion to Triple-A on August 4th, but I bet even he couldn’t have dreamt of the impact he would author. In his first MLB action in over a month, Volpe arrived in the Bronx sporting new swing mechanics and the results were immediate, the much-maligned infielder going 3-for-4 with a grand slam and a career-high five RBI. It’s his first and last ABs from that game that I would like to highlight today.We first join Volpe with no outs in the bottom of the second last Thursday against the Rockies. The Yankees need to complete the sweep and have created a promising opportunity early with Ryan McMahon singling and Austin Wells drawing a walk to open the frame. They already lead, 2-1, courtesy of a Luis García Jr. two-run blast in the first, but after Max Fried surrendered a solo shot to Kyle Karros in the second, it became imperative that the Yankees take advantage of this scoring chance given the uncertainty of how many innings they’ll get from their starter recently back from injury.Ryan Feltner starts Volpe with a first pitch sinker low hoping for an early double play ball.Really excellent take here from Volpe, this sinker looking like a strike middle-down until about the last ten feet before home. I almost wonder if he was hunting something in a different zone the way the bat never left his shoulder on such a borderline pitch. Feltner executed that sinker pretty much how he intended, so despite not getting the result he wanted, there is no need for him to deviate course. Volpe follows up that excellent take with a positively head-scratching one. This sinker looks like a strike right down the middle the moment it leaves Feltner’s hand and never leaves the zone, yet Volpe watches it all the way into the catcher’s glove for strike one.Ok, now I officially have no idea what Volpe is looking for. That’s two straight meatball sinkers from Feltner. The first he showed zero interest in offering at. This sinker is as center-cut as they come, yet all Volpe can do is fire a late emergency hack as if he is sitting on something else and gets surprised that this pitch is in a hittable location. This is a pitch he should be crushing but instead he’s swinging as if to fight it off foul to stay alive in a 1-1 count.At this point I just assumed this AB would end the way a lot of two-strike counts against Volpe end — a strikeout swinging on a breaking ball out of the zone. So far it’s been same old, same old from Volpe, failing to take advantage of mistake pitches early in the count and thus needlessly fall behind, which around these circles we know as a non-competitive AB. Feltner has been gifted an opportunity for a strikeout and his first pitch selection to get it is the changeup.Feltner misses wildly with this changeup, sailing it way up and in when he meant to locate it down below the zone. A completely non-competitive pitch and an automatic take from Volpe. Feltner immediately shelves the changeup after such a wayward misfire and switches to the secondary that has given Volpe fits his whole big league career — the low and away slider.Wow, this was… an impressively disciplined take from Volpe. This pitch looks exactly like the two in-zone sinkers that Volpe failed to punish earlier in the AB before taking a sharp left turn about halfway to the plate. You can tell that Volpe recognized the pitch pretty soon out of Feltner’s had based on the minimal flinch as he takes it for ball three.Volpe has done well to work the count full after falling behind, 1-2. Feltner does not want to walk the bases loaded with no outs and the top of the order coming up, so he is somewhat forced into throwing sinkers in the zone again in the hope of inducing a double play ball. This one lands in almost the same spot as the one Volpe took for strike one. This time he does elect to swing, but it’s not a particularly good swing. His whole front side flies open, causing the bat head to come around and over the top of the baseball, and all he can do is ground it foul to the pull side. With a swing like that, Feltner must feel confident he can get Volpe to roll over a grounder if he can command his sinker lower than the last three he threw. Instead, this sinker sails up and in just like the one changeup Feltner threw earlier. Volpe is a little unlucky that the pitch hit his bat on the check swing, otherwise he would have drawn the walk to load the bases. After showing Volpe four fastballs with sinking movement in this AB, Feltner finally breaks out the four-seamer hoping that a straight flying heater will stay above Volpe’s barrel for a strikeout. Volpe is sitting dead red, which is how he is able to make solid contact with this 95 mph four-seamer bearing in on his hands. The early swing allows him to get the bat head out and pull a sharp grounder through the hole on the left side for an RBI single to restore the Yankees’ two-run cushion. We have to fast-forward to the seventh for the real fireworks. An RBI triple by Jake McCarthy in the top-half briefly made it 4-2, but a Cody Bellinger leadoff double, Jasson Domínguez walk, and Spencer Jones two-run single provided a cushion at 6-2. McMahon and Wells then drew a pair of two-out walks to load the bases for Volpe, who steps to the plate with the confidence of a pair of singles already to his name.Unlike Feltner, Jimmy Herget looks to pitch Volpe backwards, starting with breaking balls away to slow down his bat and get him leaning out over the plate to in theory set up a heater inside later in the count. This is a perfect slider from Herget, dotted right on the corner low and away. Even though it lands for a called strike, it’s still a good take from Volpe. Had he swung, at best you’re looking at a whiff and more likely an inning ending grounder. Having earned the strike looking with that slider, Herget shows some impressive sequencing by throwing a sweeper out of the same slot — it should look like the slider Volpe just saw only this time with a foot-and-a-half more lateral movement away from the batter.This is the best take from Volpe all game and maybe all season. This sweeper comes down the exact same tunnel as the slider that was just called a strike on the outside edge. You would expect most hitters to chase this pitch — they are forced to protect that outside edge now that the pitcher has established his breaking ball for a called strike in that quadrant. Just like the close slider he took for a ball just off the plate away from Feltner, Volpe must have gotten a good read on the spin of this pitch to layoff with hardly a flinch.Despite not getting the chase, Herget sticks with his plan of soft away, hard in. He looks to bear a sinker in on Volpe’s hands for some weak contact. Instead, he leaves this 91 mph sinker middle-middle, and unlike in the first AB we covered, Volpe doesn’t miss it. Volpe stays inside the baseball and drives it to the opposite field, short porching Herget for a grand slam. The swing is a thing of beauty, Volpe precise with his barrel to the baseball while showing an impressive amount of power despite taking an opposite-field approach.The Yankees ended up routing the Rockies, 10-3, and Volpe single-handedly drove in half those runs. During the game, we learned about several mechanical adjustment Volpe implemented in his month-plus at Triple-A. I spot two major differences at the initiation of the load phase: higher hand positioning and a small step back with his back foot. Starting with the hand positioning, I feel that this helps prevent Volpe from casting his swing — you can see how before the demotion his front elbow straightens out well before contact whereas on the grand slam swing, that front elbow stays bent and tight to the body. When you straighten your front elbow too soon, your hands tend to drift away from the body, causing the bat head to lag and the swing to become long and loopy. This robs you of power, prevents you from going to the opposite field, and makes it almost impossible to catch up to the heater. Keeping the front elbow tucked leads to a shorter, more compact swing, allowing Volpe to stay inside the baseball to drive it with power the other way as the barrel rotates in sync with the torso.The adjustment that has me really excited, however, is the step back. Paul O’Neill noticed it right away on the broadcast and could not offer enough praise for the adjustment. He explained the way that that step forces Volpe to keep his weight back, allowing him to stay behind the baseball which is critical for efficiently transferring all of the stored potential energy from trunk to arms to bat. The hallmark of Volpe’s struggles is when he bails on his front side, the front hip and shoulder flying open way too early. This causes Volpe to step in the bucket, or fall with his weight toward third base rather than stride toward the pitcher, which not only robs him of power but is the prime culprit for all those whiffs against breaking balls away as Volpe deprives himself of plate coverage. This new step back is a godsend. In forcing him to keep his weight back a tick longer and stride forward instead of open, Volpe’s barrel should remain in the hitting zone for far longer than when he’s cutting across the zone when stepping in the bucket, which is how he is able to to drive a slightly inside pitch out of the park the other way.We’ve seen Volpe make mechanical adjustments in the past and then get hot for a few weeks. However, without fail he has let those past adjustments fall by the wayside and revert back to his old bad habits every single time. Hopefully, this time around these changes are here to stay.

item.title: GM gives its most important trucks a new UI—and includes CarPlay
item.author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
item.content:encoded: General Motors is about to launch new versions of its bestselling Chevrolet Silverado and GMC Sierra pickup trucks for model year 2027, and among the changes are new user interfaces for the trucks’ digital displays. The automaker has gone for a more minimalist approach than we’ve seen from it in the past, and after a demo yesterday, it seems like it has been listening to constructive feedback to improve the products. And yes, unlike GM’s electric vehicles, these trucks still let you cast your Apple or Android phone to the infotainment system.Although GM showed us video of the main instrument cluster—the gauges and info that’s presented to the driver—we don’t have any screenshots we can show you. But I was impressed with the restraint and lack of visual noise; instead, the background is always black, which should be dark even at night thanks to local dimming technology.There are a number of different views. One with simple half-moon dials for speed and engine rpm; on the right side of the display is a user-configurable zone, where you can browse your music or audio feeds, display trip info, or turn-by-turn directions. Another is a driver assist display, with green as the highlight color to show when Super Cruise is active; this shows you a representation of what the car’s fused sensors are seeing around it. A third is for off-road driving, with your various angles and diff settings, and a fourth is for towing.

item.title: No to the FIFA World Cup, yes to cycling – How the UCI Road World Championships returned to Montreal for 2026
item.author: Matilda Price
item.content:encoded: One hour. That's how long it took for a bid for the 2026 UCI Road World Championships to arrive on the mayor of Montreal's desk after city officials confirmed they wouldn't be bidding to be a host city for the 2026 FIFA World Cup. That was back in 2021. The bid was ready – it had been for years – and all the organisers needed was the green light to get the ball rolling for the first North American World Championships in 11 years.Fast forward to now, and the long-anticipated Montréal World Championships are very nearly here, but it's an event that's been in the works for much, much longer than the five years since the bid. In fact, the organisers have been dreaming about this since the very start of the Grands Prix Cyclistes de Québec and Montréal."The idea about the Worlds started maybe two or three years after [the first editions], at the third edition of the Grands Prix Cyclistes," explained the GPCQM and Worlds general manager, Joseph Limare, tracing this event's roots all the way back to 2012."It was a big challenge to have WorldTour races outside of Europe. The first year was, for all the cycling community – the WorldTour, UCI – a test. At the first edition, the teams went for maybe a kind of holiday in Canada, but after the first edition, they saw how we take care of the organisation, how we take care of the teams, about the quality of the race, and they also discovered at that time how hard the two Grands Prix Cyclistes of Québec and Montréal were. So after the first or second edition, the mindset changed."The feedback that we had after two editions was 'OK, you are in the top 10 of organisations'. And with the originality to be on a circuit, it's like the World Championships, the direction where the UCI wants to have the World Championships always finish on a circuit. So the idea came."From the seed of an idea, the planning slowly began. An early decision to make was which city might host. The World Championships had come to Montreal before in 1974, and then Hamilton in Ontario in 2003, though Montréal quite quickly became the obvious choice and they started to work out the details. "It's not the same thing [as the Grands Prix]. It's 10 times bigger than a WorldTour [race] to organise the World Championships. So after that, it was a long work about which year, where in Quebec or in Canada. We had the last edition in 2003 in Hamilton, so we needed to focus on where and when," Limare explained. "The work began at that time, and when the city of Montreal took the decision not to go with FIFA in 2021, the bid was ready on our side ... So maybe one hour after the decision of the city of Montreal not to go with FIFA, the bid was on the desk of the mayor. And after that [it was], 'OK, go', so we decided to put the bid in for 2026."Designing a distinct routeAlready WorldTour hosts for a decade, the GPCQM organisers had the confidence and backing of the UCI from very early on, who knew they could deliver a good race in Montreal. But from the start, Limare knew they didn't want to just run the Grand Prix de Montréal version 2.0 for the World Championships.Both organisationally and in terms of the sporting challenge, it needed to be different."When we jumped into the first discussion with operational people in Montreal four years ago, the first discussion was, 'OK, it's like the Grand Prix Cyclistes.' No, no, no, no, no. We had to convince them that it's not like the Grand Prix Cyclistes. It's eight days; it's 13 events."They also had certain requests from the UCI, who wanted the 2026 courses to fit into the variation of Worlds courses over the years: "The UCI asked us to have a race less difficult than last year in Kigali and less difficult than next year in Sallanches."So what they came up with was a revamped course, finishing in the iconic natural stadium that is the hilly Mount Royal park in the centre of Montreal, but with tweaked laps, and a loop out of the city that will show off parts of Montreal that the Grand Prix has never visited."We did not want 100% on the circuit, because we want to show Montréal, not just on the circuit, and involve the population," Limare said. "Cycling is a sport that is going to the population. For us, it's already easy to have people coming downtown with subways or buses and everything to come to the event, but we wanted to have more people involved because it's cycling."There's a sporting benefit to expanding outside of the circuit, too, with Limare hoping that the 12 laps, compared to the Grand Prix's 16, will change the shape of the racing."They have 16 laps for the Grand Prix Cyclistes, [which is] easier for Pogačar, for example, or that kind of rider," he said, speaking before the news that Pogačar would miss the World Championships. "But we 'only' have 12 laps for the Worlds, so it won't be as easy as it could be for Pogačar to win, because with less laps, it will open the race."Of course, as well as designing a route that was distinctive and different from the Grand Prix, Limare and his team have faced brand new challenges in organising an event as big as the World Championships. Even the matter of going beyond the main centre of Montréal is a prime example of how the challenge quickly multiplied. The main city of Montréal is an island, so to take the race off it, they obviously need to use bridges. And in Canada, bridges are under the domain of not the local government, but the federal government, so they had to work with the Canadian government from day one. Whilst some questions were an easy yes, Limare explains, other people - like the police forces outside the city who would help with security - took longer to convince.What's more, in Montréal they will host not just two road races like for the Grands Prix, but six, plus six time trials, and the mixed relay, as well as the UCI Congress. Hundreds more riders, hundreds more dignitaries, and hopefully thousands more fans. Roads need to be closed for over a week. In fact, the main finish area will be closed for more than a fortnight, straight through from the Grand Prix to the end of the Championships. In total, 36km of roads will be closed for the duration of the event - excluding the trip outside of the city - which Limare underlines as an achievement to 'only' close that many kilometres, minimising what will be a lot of disruption in the city.It's a logistical challenge ramped up to the max, and Limare points to the addition of time trials as a particular puzzle to solve, and something his organising team had never done before."We had the mountain, we had the finish, but for us, the new thing is the time trials, because with the Grand Prix Cyclistes, we don't have that kind of event," he explained. "For us, it was natural to have the time trial around the river, so we will have the time trials there, to have less elevation."Also, we have no European culture of cycling here, and we never had a time trial, for example. So for people here, it will be a new event, a time trial, they don't know, so we need to explain."Five years of official planning done, and almost 10 before that, Limare and his team have done the outreach and promotion in Europe, they've done the work in the local community, they've done the work with the city, and now all that's left is the actual event. Given how long this has been in the works, the organisers seem more than ready."So far, so good," as Limare put it.A Canadian team so good it feels plannedThe cherry on top of all of the organisers' planning is that this year will mark the first time ever that a Canadian rider comes into the World Championships as the defending champion in the road race. Magdeleine Vallieres Mill won the country's first elite road race title this time last year, putting Canadian cycling on the map in a big way and kicking off a year of hype for her home World Championships.For a plan over a decade in the making, the timing couldn't be much better. "You think it was the plan?" Limare joked. "It's really good timing, the best marketing plan that we could have with Magdeleine's victory last year. The girl power is awesome, and not only in the elite team, but for under-23 too, we know Isabella [Holmgren] will perform in under-23 too – our best chance of medals is maybe in the under-23, not elite. "Magdeleine is focused on the 26th of September; she will be at home, she will have all the support and recognition from the Montréal citizens, and all who come for the Worlds. So the timing is perfect for us."Whilst Canadian road cycling is looking the healthiest it has in a long time right now, Limare also hopes that the Worlds can contribute to that growth, as well as shining a light on what has already been achieved."We have more and more young riders, men and women, involved in cycling, more and more riders who are going to Europe for training camp or races, and this is part of what we want to celebrate with the Worlds," he said."We managed to be able to fund Cycling Canada and the Fédération Québécoise with a donation after the Worlds to be able to have more and more training camps and programmes for juniors to be able to bring them to Europe and to let them perform and understand cycling more than they can here, with more races and being more and more involved in the highest level."Considering Canada's men's football team exited the FIFA World Cup in the round of 16 earlier this summer, but their cycling stars are genuine medal contenders in multiple races next week, it certainly feels like the city of Montreal made the right call on that all-important day five years ago.Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: World’s top 20 private equity firms produce more greenhouse gases a year than most countries, report finds
item.author: Sara Sneath
item.content:encoded: Firms manage $7.3tn in assets and could afford to transition away from fossil fuels yet invest in natural gas and coal-fired plants to power datacentersThe energy portfolios of 20 private equity firms produce 1.5bn tons of greenhouse gases a year, more than the annual emissions of any country except China, the US, India and Russia, according to a new report.Together, these firms manage $7.3tn in assets of all kinds, affording them the ability to shape the pace of the transition away from fossil fuels. However their energy investments include significant fossil fuel assets including natural gas and coal-fired power plants to provide electricity to datacenters.Continue reading...

item.title: This Atlantic hurricane season is about to do something that hasn't happened in 175 years
item.author: Eric Berger
item.content:encoded: Last week, the Atlantic hurricane season blew through its traditional peak—which comes around September 10—with nary a tropical wave in sight, let alone a storm or hurricane.This is remarkable. Usually this is the time of year when sea surface temperatures reach their warmest in the tropics, and with a favorable atmosphere it should be smooth skating for tropical systems. But this year, the main region where most tropical systems develop is choked with Saharan dust and wind shear.No one is complaining. Landfalling hurricanes are incredibly destructive for coastal areas and have the potential for considerable inland rainfall. Even storms at sea, in the Gulf of Mexico, can send energy prices skyrocketing—the last thing needed this year.

item.title: Tom Pidcock, Zoe Bäckstedt, Cat Ferguson lead the line as Great Britain confirms squads for UCI Road World Championships
item.author: Patrick Fletcher
item.content:encoded: GB is one of the last major nations to announce its line-ups for the eight days of racing that begin this coming Sunday, but it has now revealed what performance director Stephen Park describes as "a highly competitive squad". Tom Pidcock leads the line in the elite men's road race, the 27-year-old star a genuine contender in a field blown open by the absence of the reigning champion Tadej Pogačar. Adam Yates, a decorated hilly Classics rider and a teammate of Pogačar's at UAE Team Emirates-XRG, will also enjoy a protected leadership role, while the rest of the squad is geared towards support roles. Oscar Onley has been included after placing fifth overall at the Vuelta a España, as has a breakout star from the Spanish Grand Tour, Callum Thornley, who came within a whisker of winning the stage 18 time trial. National road race champion Fred Wright has made the boat, as have Mark Donovan, Finlay Pickering, and James Shaw. Ethan Hayter, who almost beat Pogačar to win the short opening time trial at the Vuelta, has also been included in the elite men's squad but only for the time trial, where Thornley will take the other of the two spots. As for the elite women's squad, Backstedt takes aim at both the road race and the time trial as she steps up to the elite level for the first time at the World Championships. Still only 21, she pulled off the junior road race and time trial world title double in 2022, and she won the U23 time trial world title last year. Now, she steps up to lead the line at the highest level.Backstedt is joined in the elite women's road race squad by Lauren Dickson, who has impressed in the service of Demi Vollering at FDJ United-SUEZ this season, and by the former Paris-Roubaix podium finisher Pfeiffer Georgi. Josie Nelson, Flora Perkins, and Anna Henderson round out the six-woman road race squad.Despite being the Olympic silver medallist in the discipline, Henderson will not take the second time trial spot alongside Bäckstedt; instead that goes to a surprise selection in Anna Morris. The Welshwoman is primarily known for her exploits on the track and doesn't ride for an international road team, but was second in the national championships time trial in June and has earned a call-up to her first Road World Championships at the age of 31.The big British prospect, Cat Ferguson returns to action after a long injury lay-off to target rainbow jerseys in the U23 ranks. Ferguson did the road race - time trial double at junior level in 2024, two years after Bäckstedt, and turned pro with Movistar the following year.Her 2026 campaign started strongly, but she has not raced since fracturing her ankle on the opening day of the Giro d'Italia Women in late May.In the men's U23 ranks, Ben Wiggins will ride the time trial as well as the road race, where Elliot Rowe, who was the best young rider at the recent Tour of Britain, is one to watch.Ethan Hayter (time trial only)Callum Thornley (road race + time trial)Zoe Bäckstedt (road race + time trial)Anna Morris (time trial only)Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: Exclusive: Paying for frontier AI models buys 4-month head start at 5x the cost
item.author: Jeremy Hsu
item.content:encoded: The performance gap between frontier AI models from US tech companies and the best open-weights models from Chinese companies has closed to just 4.4 months, according to a Mozilla report. That explains why many companies are shifting to the significantly cheaper open models for routine work—and helps reveal a narrow band of workloads where frontier models are worth the cost.Most organizations should ideally be using open models as the default for the majority of their work, according to the latest State of Open Source AI report from Mozilla, published on September 15 and shared with Ars prior to publication. The report highlights how a leading open model, Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, achieves a composite AI performance score on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index that is just three points behind Anthropic’s Fable 5 closed frontier model, all while costing just 30 percent of the latter.“[A Closed model] earns its premium in a few places: expert professional work, high-intensity retrieval, and long context,” Raffi Krikorian, chief technology officer at Mozilla, said in an email to Ars. “We see the decision to pay for closed [models] as workload-specific rather than organization-specific.”

item.title: The Yankees have found a way in 2026
item.author: Madison Pavich
item.content:encoded: The Yankees will officially be playing baseball in October after last night’s loss by Toronto, shortly followed by New York’s own win allowing for a more raucous celebration rather than a somber one. It has not come easily for them this year, as they’ve weathered more than their fair share of blows to key players and endured lengthy slumps from others, but the man who has stood at the helm all year coasted them through to the starting line once again.I’m not one to subscribe to the notion that managers strongly impact the game positively or negatively, but Aaron Boone has been a lightning rod for criticism throughout his tenure in New York for a whole host of reasons out of his control on top of some that he does hold some influence over, so I think it’s only fair to give him some credit for what has been an incredibly difficult season to navigate. Losing Aaron Judge to start June and not getting him back until September was a severe blow to the team, as it would’ve been at any point over the last near decade, and the offense withered without him for a long while. Unlike when he went down in 2023, however, this year’s Yankees didn’t collapse with the captain out of commission, and though they tried their hardest to make the games frustrating they managed to walk the tightrope convincingly enough to stay afloat in the standings.You could certainly credit a large portion of that success to a stronger and deeper rotation this season compared to when they were rolling out Gerrit Cole and a bunch of bodies and I’d agree, but there’s been turmoil there too as injuries continually prevented the Yankees from lining up their five best starters in a given turn through the order. On top of that, the pitching staff as a whole was a little suspect with a bullpen that many questioned at the start of the year — for good reason as it turned out. David Bednar was unquestioned as the closer, though he struggled out of the gate, but the bridge to Bednar was rickety and swinging on frayed rope at the start of the year. Fernando Cruz was a solid option who earned some late-inning appearances, but unfortunately an elbow injury has put his season (and perhaps Yankees career) in jeopardy. Camilo Doval was the initial setup man, but he turned out to be a bust in pinstripes and there were only question marks surrounding the rest of the relief corps. The emergence of Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick forming the big three at the back of the ‘pen quite possibly is the biggest reason that this team is leading the Wild Card standings with a shot at the division still, their lock-down performances holding slim lead after slim lead and putting out fires whenever called upon having bailed out an offense that looked downright putrid for weeks. Boone has rarely leaned so heavily on a pair of arms before, but he’s fitted the two into the Scott Proctor mold and reaped the rewards for doing so while seemingly keeping them fresh enough as we enter the final stretch of the regular season.The bullpen management has been his biggest success, but Boone and the front office have pushed the right buttons in a number of areas. The team was getting nothing out of the catcher position offensively in the first half of the year, but they surprised many by not acquiring a catcher at the Trade Deadline and instead affirming their faith in Austin Wells, who shepherded the pitchers well enough but had been absolutely dreadful with the bat. He turned around and gave them a respectable July before hitting above-average in August, and though he’s gone through another slump in September he’s still become more than respectable in the lineup again. Wells is far from the only regular they’ve been rewarded for believing in — Jazz Chisholm Jr. endured a topsy-turvy season that drew plenty of criticism after he put a goal of 50 home runs and 50 steals on his shoulders in spring. The homers never came close as he hit only six through the first two months, but Jazz has gotten close on the basepaths with 40 stolen bags this year. The option of flipping Chisholm ahead of his impending free agency was floated in trade rumors but never emerged, and instead he’s turned in a season that will end up coming close to his previous two years by fWAR.The only real shakeup that Brian Cashman made to this roster came at the deadline, where the team traded for Luis García Jr. and Heliot Ramos — a pair of platoon bats, though García was the big get having led the National League in slugging when he was moved and has played accordingly since. From within they called up George Lombard Jr. and sent Anthony Volpe down to Triple-A to work on his maligned offensive capabilities while also considering new positions. Both moves paid dividends, with Lombard providing a spark and an injection of youth to the lineup while Volpe got a hero’s return on Thursday when he hit a grand slam against the Rockies and received a curtain call from the fans. I can’t imagine that when Volpe was demoted he was ever significantly in the team’s immediate plans for the rest of the year, but injuries again pressed them and their choice to finally allow Volpe the space to work on his craft has paid off with him sliding into second base in Chisholm’s absence.There’s a dozen points where this season could’ve gone up in flames for the Yankees, but here they stand in the middle of September with a ticket to at least two guaranteed games of postseason baseball with the potential for more. The division is still within their grasp even if time is running out, and they simply can’t control how well the Rays have played. They can only handle their own business, and they’ve done a phenomenal job of doing just that this year.

item.title: Enric Mas' maturity and calmness allowed him to capitalise on strong form, while his GC rivals have plenty of lessons to learn from the Vuelta a España – Philippa York analysis
item.author: Philippa York
item.content:encoded: After years of trying, the final week of the season's last Grand Tour has finally delivered satisfaction to three different riders in remarkably similar circumstances. Not that they could have been entirely certain at the start of the third week that by the end of this Vuelta a España they would be on the podium at all.The most likely of the trio to predict success was always going to be Enric Mas, who since the exit of Tadej Pogačar on stage 8 had stepped into the role of race leader with remarkable maturity. Having finished runner-up on three other occasions, it no doubt gave him insight into how the race could be won, but having come so close before, there would have been some doubts that misfortune might rear its ugly head in the remaining days. Movistar have a track record of messing up tactics, neglecting inter-team relationships and stifling ambitions to satisfy others’ egos – these issues were certainly in my mind while watching along. Surprisingly, there were no tantrums or drama as the days ticked by and the pressure mounted; this remained a Movistar squad in complete agreement that the mission was to have Enric Mas in the maillot rojo at the conclusion of stage 21. Not by chance or good fortune or anything random, but by hard work, good tactical moves and believing that this was the year the Mallorcan, so often the plucky challenger, was the most complete of the GC riders.Having watched previous editions of La Vuelta where the Spanish squad managed to remove all confidence from their best riders, it has been refreshing to see them learn from past errors and actually solidify around their team leader. Already being the strongest climber of the GC group helped, but Mas producing a time trial performance that probably surprised even himself made the task of deciphering the two remaining mountain days so much easier. It also put more pressure on Primož Roglič and Felix Gall's shoulders, as they weren’t really fighting for the overall victory anymore; instead, they had to focus on each other. A Grand Tour of learning for several GC contendersFor sure, Primož Roglič was going to try; the four-time champion knew how to win the overall, but the problem was the legs weren’t where he needed them to be for a spectacular reversal. However, the Slovenian has to be happy with his return from the injury that hampered his preparation in the run-up to the start in Monaco. He showed, despite his 36 years, that he still is a force to be reckoned with and didn’t put a foot wrong in the three weeks of racing. Still ambitious, still competitive and a presence not to be dismissed. Felix Gall, on the other hand, finished La Vuelta seemingly content with his lot, which you can’t argue with if you look at just the result. However, the manner in which Decathlon CMA CGM operated does raise several questions. Before the start, they would have immediately signed up for a podium place, understandably so, but when Pogačar left the race, the French squad didn’t seem to realise that they were competing for the overall title. Gall lacked race craft, attacking at the wrong moments, missing moves when he ought to have been vigilant and generally accepting that he was doing rather well and that was good enough. The killer instinct Mas and Roglič possessed was absent from the Austrian. Already this season, at the Giro d’Italia, he had the opportunity to learn from Jonas Vingegaard about the art of dispatching rivals. But the lesson didn’t seem to have sunk in between the two events. His and Decathlon’s Vuelta is a case of what might have been if they had a bit more ambition and clarity in the crucial moments. The final mountain-top finish was an example of what might have been if only Gall had committed earlier, and had he spent decent time on his TT bike, then he wouldn’t have lost so much time so needlessly. He has the power but not the position to guarantee an acceptable performance. It might seem a harsh judgement, but all the riders he is competing with are better than him because, as he has said, he doesn’t like the discomfort of time trialling. A strange observation, considering there’s no such thing as a comfortable TT. Richard Carapaz had a similarly average individual TT, but he countered that by being aggressive and using his experience to exploit the close marking between the top three. A bigger contrast in race craft and tactics you’ll rarely see from two teams closely matched – EF Education-EasyPost were always looking for and aware of opportunities whilst Decathlon CMA CGM retreated to defensive racing and, in the process, did a lot of the work they could have passed on to Movistar.The French squad always blinked first when there were any hesitations, and as the race went on, everyone knew they would. Conversely, Movistar never really put a foot wrong. For a long time it looked like Netcompany-Ineos had a rider capable of following Mas and company when they lit up the race, but ultimately Oscar Onley lacked last season's form from mid-race onwards. His TT was where it was expected to be, at just under a minute behind Roglič. However, the last two mountain stages were fatal to his podium chances. Whether it was too many setbacks, lingering effects of his early illness or a level of climbing that was a little bit too fast for him, Onley wasn’t where we thought he might be. The Vuelta demanded a degree of explosiveness, and the young Scot just didn’t have enough left by the end. In contrast, Sepp Kuss never really entered the GC equation until the penultimate day and then jumped six places after slumbering outside the top-10 for most of the last week. This wasn’t vintage Kuss on spectacular form, though; he used his experience, tenacity and the collective strength of Visma-Lease a Bike to drag himself into the top five. This season is the second time he’s ridden all three Grand Tours, so you can excuse him for taking longer to get going and, unlike in 2023 when he won, the Dutch team were here with Wout Van Aert and Matthew Brennan to look after too. The GC was always going to be an extra cherry on top of their sprint ambitions. They won’t be complaining after five stage wins for the young Brit and two victories and the points classification for the Belgian. Both of them were in epic form throughout.Another Slovenian talent shines at La VueltaAlso epic was Santiago Buitrago, who sought out the mountains classification and saw off the challenge of Van Aert but didn’t get his stage win despite being in all the right breaks. Done over by Marco Brenner in the second week and again by Eddie Dunbar in the third, at least it all turned out okay in the end, which wasn’t the case for Dunbar, who crashed on the dangerous approach to the final big climb of the race. The race organisers will have noted the lack of respect. The Swiss TT specialist beating Callum Thornley was almost forgivable until he packed his bags and scarpered. Someone who did need to leave early was Mattias Skjelmose. He ought to have followed Mads Pedersen’s example and gone home to recover instead of flogging himself for a GC position he never looked likely to reach. Lidl-Trek had a below-par race by their standards. As ever, there were some surprises. Cofidis and Bryan Coquard were competitive, and it’s been a while since that happened, and Groupama-FDJ United, not to be left out, also won a bunch sprint with Bastien Tronchon – a mini French revival in a race where they are often bystanders. Jakob Omrzel appeared on our radar, looking very much like the next Slovenian youngster to amaze everyone. Only two riders in the overall top-10 won a stage: Enric Mas and Omrzel, who finished sixth overall, pushing Onley for the white jersey. He was decidedly nonplussed by his performances – quite remarkable and reminiscent of a certain Pogacar who first showed at the Spanish Grand Tour.Uno-X Mobility did what they always do – organised, aggressive, but it hasn’t always paid off as well as it did at this Vuelta, with Andreas Leknessund outlasting Wout van Aert in the opening week after a ridiculously hard day out, and Tobias Johannessen finishing things off in Granada whole holding off another of the new names to watch, Alessandro Romele. And finally, to go with the feeling that this edition was a Spanish fiesta, Mikel Landa won the big mountain stage, easily the hardest day and raced until everyone finished on their knees. Landa is heading back to his roots at Euskaltel next season – tears of joy and relief in equal measure. From being a Tadej Pogačar benefit race, the 81st Vuelta a España turned into a properly entertaining contest between riders not that far apart in ability. Enric Mas won because he had the best team, good tactics and a level of calm that let him exploit his return to top form.

item.title: Yankees prospects: Week 25 minor league recap
item.author: Michael Zeno
item.content:encoded: We’ve reached the final stretch, folks. One week from today, we could be completely done with minor league baseball. Hudson Valley concluded a week ago, Somerset concluded on Sunday, Tampa will conclude on Wednesday at the latest, and Scranton will need a huge week to see their season go past this coming Sunday.As we begin to wind down the minor league recaps, we bid adieu to the 2026 Somerset Patriots while checking in on the RailRiders’ playoff push and Tampa’s journey to an FSL championship.Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders 38-30 (75-66), 2 GB in the International League East after a 2-4 week against the Rochester Red Wings (Nationals) +55 (+58)Home vs. Jacksonville Jumbo Shrimp (Marlins)That’s a back-breaking week for the RailRiders’ playoff hopes. They entered the week in a dead draw with Rochester, so whoever won this series was going to have the definitive advantage heading into the final week. Almost every game could’ve gone both ways, but they’re going to really be hurting over Saturday and Sunday, blowing a 6-0 lead in the former and coming up short on a late rally in the latter. They’ll now need to pick up three games in the last week to make the playoffs.It was a pretty meh week for the offense, with the exception of some late-week heroics by Oswaldo Cabrera (multi-homer game on Sunday) and Marco Luciano (homered in consecutive games). We also saw Duke Ellis surpass 50 stolen bases, continuing a remarkable streak of baserunning excellence. It truly is something to behold how many guys down here have major league experience and prior notoriety, and that’s not even counting Mitch Garver, who continues to be in limbo after neither the Yankees nor anyone else wanted to add him to their active roster before the September 1st deadline. Not sure what’s going on there.As for the rotation, Alexander Cornielle drew double duty and continued his strong stretch on Monday before struggling on Sunday. Elmer Rodríguez tossed four shutout innings before getting blown up in the fifth on Friday, while Kyle Carr and Xavier Rivas continued to do their piggyback system, with the latter picking up his first Triple-A win with five solid innings. Once again, Brendan Beck was the standardbearer of the week, tossing 5.1 shutout innings to continue one of the best years by a minor league starter this season. Funny enough, the Yankees have the only two starters with a sub-3 ERA and 100 innings at the level: him and Elmer.As you might expect from a bad week, the bullpen didn’t do its job. Eric Reyzelman and Chris Kean both tossed two scoreless innings, but the veterans weren’t as sharp, namely Justin Topa, Yerry de los Santos, and Eli Morgan. .283/.361/.420, 7 HR, 30 RBI, 14 SB, 107 wRC+ .277/.377/.483, 16 HR, 50 RBI, 29 XBH, 125 wRC+.289/.346/.447, 19 HR, 69 RBI, 34 XBH, 106 wRC+ 10-2, 2.75 ERA, 3.19 FIP, 1.03 WHIP, 20.6 K-BB% (131 IP)8-4, 2.48 ERA, 3.71 FIP, 1.29 WHIP, 12.4 K-BB% (101.2 IP)Double 37-32 (74-64), 3.5 GB in the Eastern League Northeast after a 4-2 week against the Hartford Yard Goats (Rockies) +9 (+45)Somerset’s season came to an end this week after going 4-2 against Hartford. They played too mediocre over the last several weeks to make a serious playoff push, and wound up playing out the string this week with a group that looked a helluva lot different than the offensive juggernaut they had on Opening Day.We saw great finishes to the season by Core Jackson and Roderick Arias, two guys who’ve had chaotic seasons. Jackson had three different IL stints, while Arias had a nightmarish start before completely saving his prospect stock with an incredible finish. The two constants at this level all season were Jace Avina and Coby Morales. The former was incredible through the end of July but had a tough end to the season. Morales was incredibly consistent from start to finish as a 20/20 bat, having found a power stroke that eluded him early in his pro career.On the pitching side, it’s a season of disappointment. Ben Hess only pitched 56.2 innings before going on the injured list; Cade Smith had a tumultuous and inconsistent season; and the rotation spent much of the last several weeks being heavily reliant on bullpen games. Two late call-ups really opened some eyes, though. Bryce Cunningham finished strong in what felt like a lost season for a while, and Rory Fox capped his first pro season with 7.2 scoreless innings this past week and a 3.97 ERA across 47.2 innings post-promotion. Ultimately, there’s a bunch of players here who we could see in Scranton next year, but also a handful I’d expect to start next year in Somerset, namely Arias, Jackson, Cunningham, and Fox. We’ll see if they’re joined by some aggressive promotions lower on the farm. .254/.350/.467, 20 HR, 65 RBI, 50 XBH, 120 wRC+ .263/.325/.485, 23 HR, 85 RBI, 49 XBH, 113 wRC+ .282/.372/.479, 21 HR, 81 RBI, 21 SB, 129 wRC+ 8-5, 4.36 ERA, 3.87 FIP, 1.26 WHIP, 17.5 K-BB% (130 IP)Bryce Cunningham (A+/AA): 4-9, 4.61 ERA, 4.56 FIP, 1.30 WHIP, 12.6 K-BB% (105.1 IP)High-A Hudson Valley RenegadesMissed playoffs. Down 1-0 to Jupiter in FSL Championship SeriesGames 2 and 3 of FSL Championship Series vs. Jupiter Hammerheads (Marlins)Tampa played just three games this week, breezing past Clearwater in a two-game sweep to get to the FSL Championship Series. They lost Game 1 of that series, 9-1, in a game that was blown open in the ninth via a seven spot. They’ll have to win the next two, which doesn’t seem impossible for the hottest team in Single-A, which swept Jupiter in a five-game series at the end of August.Game 1 against Clearwater was a sleepy 2-0 win. Both runs were scored off a rehabbing Nestor Cortes, with the RBI knocks coming from Yostin Pena (2-3, RBI, BB, R, SB) and Paul Gutierrez-Contreras II (1-3, RBI, 2B). J.T. Etheridge tossed five shutout innings to continue an incredible last few weeks, while being backed up by sharp relief from Antonio Gomez, Jose Ledesma, and Matthew Tippie.Game 2 was higher scoring, but also more tense. Gutierrez-Contreras blasted a fourth-inning homer, but the team trailed 3-2 after seven. Hoping to finish things off quickly, Pena ripped an RBI double off the wall in center field before Wilberson De Pena crushed a go-ahead home run. Add a two-run single by Tyce Armstrong, and they had what they needed to win, even with Tippie’s ninth-inning struggles. Tyler Boudreau returned after taking a nasty comebacker last week and struck out nine in five innings, but had to settle for a no-decision in a 7-5 win to secure the sweep.In Game 1 of the FSL Championship Series on Sunday, this dynamic offense was completely silenced aside from a Luis Escudero home run in the eighth inning. Justin West tossed five shutout innings to continue his strong second half by him, but the bullpen allowed nine runs in the final few innings. item.title: Lazer Verde Keneticore helmet review: An eco-conscious model for e-bike riders
item.author: Simon Lock
item.content:encoded: 481g / 17oz (size M-L) S-M (50-56cm) amd M-L (55-61cm)4 out of 5YesMatte Lemongrass, Matte White Stone, Matte Sage Green, Matte Fort Knox, Matte Grey OnyxDespite the e-bike helmet being a relatively new subgenre in the world of bike apparel, there are already plenty of good options – see our best e-bike helmets guide for more of them. You probably have a list of must-haves when it comes to making a purchase: safety, comfort, and not looking daft. Sustainability credentials may or may not sway your final decision, but if you are looking for a model that looks after both your head and the planet, the Lazer Verde KinetiCore is for you. Having used the Verde on both my 40-minute pedal-powered commute and on weekend e-bike outings for many weeks now, I can vouch for it as a comfortable, stylish option that won’t break the bank. At the time of writing, I haven’t put its safety credentials or ease of recycling to the test, but the relevant certificates and documentation back those up. Lazer have been making helmets for over 100 years and claims to have designed the first true hardshell helmet, so it has always put technical innovation at the heart of its design. The Verde is the latest product of this ethos, being the first to feature the brand’s EcoLoc system, which allows the helmet to be disassembled and recycled after use. In fact, 70 per cent of the helmet’s weight is made from recycled materials. There is no glue, Velcro, paint or stickers, all of which make the helmet’s production and decommissioning much less harmful to the planet. Eco credentials in cycle kit can often read like marketing guff rather than genuinely meaningful action, but this doesn’t feel like the case with the Verde. Its closest competitor in the sustainable e-bike helmet category (admittedly a pretty niche genre) is probably the POC Myelin, however, the POC doesn’t have nearly as much certification. The Verde comes with the essential NTA 8776 certificate, which is a Dutch standard specifically for e-bikes that rubber-stamps the helmet’s ability to perform in higher-speed collisions. It was awarded 4 out of 5 stars from Virginia Tech, so isn’t quite as safe as they come, but it’s pretty good. The helmet uses Lazer’s KinetiCore (essentially an in-house alternative to the MIPS design), which uses crumple zones rather than a separate inner shell like MIPS. The Verde claims to provide ventilation that both offers enough inflow to keep you cool, while simultaneously keeping rain out. This is achieved by having most of the vents in the shell and the liner seemingly misaligned, which looks slightly odd at first glance. The cradle uses Lazer's TurnSys dial adjuster, but unlike some of the brand's alternative options, there is no lateral adjustment. The strap comes with the old-school pinch-release buckle where some of the Verde’s competitors opt for a magnetic clasp, but again the design leans towards simplicity over sophistication as a way to reduce waste, and I’m here for it. The Verde doesn’t come with a visor or the means to attach one. In terms of customisation, you might want to consider attaching Lazer’s LED light. There’s also the brand's compatible Winter Kit, which connects to the inside of the helmet to add insulation for colder commutes. Given the reduced ventilation, however, you might not need any extra warmth. There are five matte colourways to choose from, with the Sage Green and Fort Knox particularly catching the eye. Another thing to note regarding the colour is that the plastic isn’t painted (another eco decision), it’s dyed, and has proved more resistant to scratches so far. Otherwise, the design is pretty slick and isn’t as bulky as some of its peers. Overall, the Verde performed pretty well during test rides, which consisted of both e-bike nursery drop-offs and 40-minute, non–pedal-assisted commutes into the office. It’s probably worth noting that all of this riding was done in the south of England during the long, hot summer of 2026. The two main things that let the Verde down are its noticeable weight and insufficient ventilation. While it feels unfair to judge it too harshly during the hottest British summer on record, for me the ventilation wasn’t sufficient for medium effort or on a warm day, and after half an hour I could feel the weight on my head – unlike my ususal helmet. In designing the vents to keep rain out, it feels as though Lazer have sacrificed too much in the way of airflow. If you’re the sort of e-bike rider who is happy to let your battery do most of the work, then this might not be a concern, but if you’re looking for an all-rounder that you can use at the weekend on longer rides, then you might want to shop around. In terms of weight, the M-L Verde comes in at nearly half a kilo which, given it doesn’t come with in-built smart features or a visor, feels quite weighty. Compared to the similar Smith Dispatch, it’s around 100g heavier. Again, if you are using pedal-assist, keeping to shorter distances and riding in an upright position, this is much less of an issue. I noticed the weight far more when I was commuting head-down on my Genesis Croix de Fer compared to the rides when sat up straight on my motor-equipped Tern Quick Haul.Having stripped the design back to make it more sustainable, there’s an unfussiness to the Verde that is quite refreshing. The TurnSys dial adjuster feels a bit primitive at first but is actually really effective and robust. The lack of lateral adjustment leaves you a bit limited when it comes to catering for ponytails or just getting a customised fit. The straps feel a little bit dated but work well and are simple to adjust once the helmet is in place, although come with a pinch-release buckle and without any chin strap pads or the like. While the lack of glue in the manufacturing process means the shell and the liner are not inseparable and feel slightly loose on occasion, knowing this is part of the eco-friendly design put my mind at rest.Lazer haven’t gone overboard on the padding, having sacrificed both glue and Velcro in an effort to make the helmet more recyclable. One inadvertent positive of having less padding is that when things do get a bit sweaty, is that there's less material to soak it up.Otherwise, the overall fit was fine, even for someone not blessed with the most conventional-shaped head. Trying on helmets is not something I relish, as they usually only accentuate my Frank Sidebottom-esque aesthetic, but the Verde doesn’t look overly bulky. Even in the larger M-L sizing, the helmet doesn't look excessive. The choice of matte colours is also very easy on the eye. I didn’t fall in love with the Lemongrass option of my test helmet, but I very much like the look of the Sage Green and Fort Knox.Anyone who is accustomed to making climate-conscious purchasing decisions knows that they often incur something of a surcharge. The Verde feels firmly in that category, given both its weight and its stripped-back design feel like they could belong to a slightly cheaper helmet. But for those who genuinely try and make impactful choices when buying kit, the extra outlay might feel warranted. The Verde comes in slightly cheaper than the POC Myelin (at full price) and has much greater protection certification. The simple straps without chinstraps or magnetic clasp feel slightly outdated, not to mention out of place at this price point, but won’t ultimately have a huge impact on the important things like safety and comfort. At £99, the Verde comes in considerably more expensive than some of the best e-bike helmets, like the Specialized Mode, which has a similar stylish design and all the safety certification you need. If you’d prefer some lighting already integrated, the Nutcase Vio comes is at a similar price but has 360-degree lighting and uses MIPS technology rather than Lazer’s KinetiCore. If you have room in the budget, there are a number of options around the £150 mark that weigh in quite a bit lighter, have integrated lights and much improved ventilation. Overall, the Verde is a solid and aesthetically-pleasing option that will keep your head intact should the worst happen. It also comes with the added benefit of helping you sleep better at night knowing you’re doing your bit for the environment. The insufficient ventilation and weight of the helmet might leave you a bit hot and bothered if you’re putting in a decent amount of effort or you’re out on a warm day for more than 30 minutes, but for the average e-bike commute or school run, you should be OK. There are arguably better value helmets on the market, but that depends what price you put on sustainable design. There are also helmets that come with more bells and whistles, like integrated lights, but the simplicity of the adjustment on both the cradle and straps might suit the purists out there. As much as an e-bike helmet purchase should fundamentally be about protecting your grey matter on the road, even the most safety-conscious of us want to look nice at the same time. The Verde is a good-looking lid that isn’t overly bulky and it comes in five great colours. Testing scorecard and notesFits well although uses minimal padding and is quite heavyComes with the NTA 8776 but only 4 out of 5 on Virginia TechNot sufficient for hot days or tough ridesSustainable, stylish and great colour optionsEco-conscious approach means minimal features

item.title: 'My good shape will come in handy with sitting on the couch' - Injury forces Mischa Bredewold out of Road World Championships
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: Bredewold was taking part in the four-day race in the Ardèche region of France when she crashed on the opening stage, sustaining a minor fracture to her pelvis and an injury to her elbow. Though she managed to remount and finish the stage, 10 minutes behind the winner, a hospital visit revealed the injuries.Her SD Worx-Protime teammate Mikayla Harvey went down in the same incident, abandoned immediately and has since been diagnosed with a concussion. While Bredewold has since undergone successful surgery on her injuries, the Dutch cycling federation has since announced Amber Kraak will take her place on the Montreal start line."Went to the hospital after a crash in Ardèche tour for a few stitches, went home with a ischiopubic (pelvic) fracture and surgery on my elbow wound," Bredewold wrote in an Instagram post."Unexpected turn of events, and beyond disappointment. Big goals were coming with Worlds in Montreal and Worlds on the track in China, which I both felt very ready for."I will need some time to process this big big big disappointment and to heal up, luckily my good shape will come in handy with sitting on the couch. I’m lucky to have people around me close to my heart at a time like this.. Thanks to my lovely teammates. I’ll be back!!!!! Trust the process…"Bredewold is an excellent all-rounder and would have proved av strong backup for Dutch team leader Demi Vollering in the Worlds road race, which will be held on Saturday, September 26 in Montreal. Starting her career at Parkhotel Valkenburg in 2021, Bredewold joined SD Worx two years later and has bagged a total of 23 victories. Though she missed out on winning a fourth successive Classic Lorient Agglomération recently, finishing second, 2026 has been another good year for the 26-year-old.After bagging a stage of La Vuelta Femenina, she won the opening day at Itzulia Women, defending doggedly to win the GC before taking another stage win at the Vuelta a Burgos Feminas.Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: Audi's shrewd choice of F2 team for its first F1 junior
item.author: Josh Suttill
item.content:encoded: Audi's first Formula 1 junior driver Freddie Slater will join forces with defending champion team Invicta in Formula 2 in 2027.Slater narrowly missed out on the Formula 3 title at the Madring last weekend but has had a highly impressive rookie season, living up to the promise built up by strong karting success and back-to-back titles in Italian Formula 4 and the Formula Regional European Championship.It was that early-career success that meant he had offers from multiple F1 teams to join their junior programmes from an early age.But much like Max Verstappen and Lando Norris, Slater and his management team held off on accepting those offers too early.At the start of this year, he accepted Audi's proposal for him to become the first driver to join its F1 driver development programme as it entered F1 in 2026.Slater fell 14 points short of winning the F3 title, having suffered a costly mechanical failure in the Monza feature race and a nightmare Madrid title-decider that allowed chief rival Ugo Ugochukwu to take the crown instead.Slater will now move up to F2 with Invicta, the team that has taken back-to-back championship doubles in the last two years, with Audi F1 driver Gabriel Bortoleto and McLaren reserve driver Leonardo Fornaroli taking the last two drivers’ titles with it. Bortoleto and Fornaroli both also went from Trident's F3 team to Invicta's F2 team, just as Slater will.Invicta is currently hoping to make it three out of three F2 titles this year with Ferrari junior Rafael Camara, who is seven points adrift of championship leader Nikola Tsolov. Invicta itself is also just six points off Campos in the teams' title race.F2 has added an extra feature race to its next round in Baku amid uncertainty over its current final two rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.Slater is set to make his debut in the post-season Abu Dhabi test, although this will likely have to be rescheduled if F1 cancels its Qatar and Abu Dhabi weekends as expected. F2 could decide to join F1 if it holds its season finale at Imola in December, as is the current back-up plan. Logically the post-season F2 test would also be held there."The move to Formula 2 is the natural next step for Freddie, and an important new phase of his development as a driver," Audi's driver development director Allan McNish said."He enjoyed a strong Formula 3 season, fighting for the title until the final round - showing his speed, racecraft and progress throughout the year."We are very proud of what Freddie has achieved this season and how he has developed along the way. Invicta Racing has had an excellent record in recent years, and we are delighted to be working with them."We believe it is the ideal environment for him, and we look forward to supporting him as he takes on this new challenge in 2027."Invicta has been the clear benchmark team during the three years of F2's current car, but the series is introducing a heavily revised version of the car from 2027.Slater was present at the launch of the new car at Monza, telling The Race: "I think it's mega. I think it's very exciting."Obviously F1 has changed a lot this year so F2 kind of needs to follow suit to progress to that ladder."So I'm very excited to get a go behind the wheel of one and it's going to be very interesting to see what it performs like."Slater is the first confirmed 2027 F2 driver, but he’s expected to be joined by a number of his F3 rivals, including champion Ugochukwu.A second-place championship finish in F3 and titles in F4 and FREC mean Slater, who is yet to drive an F1 car, has more than enough points to clear the 40-point threshold for an F1 superlicence.

item.title: Fast, furious and potentially fatal: why are supercars suddenly so popular?
item.author: Steve Rose
item.content:encoded: Once the preserve of the ultra-rich, supercars are finding new drivers through rentals, finance deals, influencer culture and the manosphere. But why would anyone want a 200mph vehicle?‘The £600,000 Lamborghini; that was the first seizure of the operation,” says special chief inspector Geoff Tatman of the Metropolitan police, thinking back to the second weekend of August. “He was stopping at the red lights, revving his engine, waiting for the traffic to clear, then speeding. So on the third time we saw him do it, we stopped him and seized the vehicle.” The car has a top speed of 217mph (350kmh), but the limit on these London streets is 20mph. Over the same weekend, the Metropolitan police seized about 90 more cars with a combined value of more than £8m, an increase on last year’s tally of 72 cars. They were seized for various offences: driving without insurance, driving with incorrect licences or antisocial behaviour. Previously, the Met would have had to let such drivers off with a warning, but the law – section 59 of the Police Reform Act – was strengthened this year to enable the immediate confiscation of vehicles. The seized cars also included a Ferrari Monza worth about £3.4m (the driver only had a provisional UK licence). They were all put on display at Marble Arch, attracting a throng of camera-wielding onlookers (one attender did a seven-hour live blog of the occasion).Many of the supercars apprehended by the Met in August bore Middle Eastern number plates. It has been a growing trend for car owners from the region to spend summer in London, bringing their cars with them (at a cost of £25,000 upwards). The orange Lamborghini that Tatman seized had Dubai plates. Most of the vehicle owners retrieved their cars the next day after paying fines and presenting the correct paperwork. The Lamborghini driver was subsequently seen driving respectfully and not revving his engine. Lessons were learned, although the question remains: why ship a 200mph car to London to drive in a 20mph zone?Continue reading...

item.title: 'I was surprised as well' - Movistar general manager Eusebio Unzué analyses Enric Mas' unexpected but welcome victory in Vuelta a España
item.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
item.content:encoded: The barricades from the Vuelta a España's final stage have been cleared away in Granada now, and the water in the fountain in the Paseo del Salón boulevard where the final victory celebrations took place is no longer tinged with red dye to reflect the colour of the Vuelta leader's jersey.But the consequences of a race won by Enric Mas in the least expected circumstances - following a crash-out by Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) - has brought a fresh Grand Tour triumph to Movistar, and will take much longer to be fully absorbed.The 2026 Vuelta is the fifth in the history of the team co-created by Eusebio Unzué back in 1980, and its first since 2016 with Nairo Quintana. It's also Spain's first victory in its home race since 2014. Enric Mas made the podium four times, but never the top place until now.That all changed on Sunday, when Mas, who had suffered thrombophlebitis a year ago in July and endured a miserable debut in the 2026 Giro d'Italia, was able to turn the tables on his season and his entire career by claiming his first-ever Grand Tour. All this at 31, too. After inheriting the jersey from Pogačar on stage 8, and winning on the Alto de Aitana on stage 9, he continued outgunning or equalling his rivals on every summit finish that followed, keeping the opposition at a safe distance when riding the time trial of his life on stage 18.The triumph for Movistar represents a massive boost for Mas, the Movistar team and Spanish cycling. As Unzué, the sport's longstanding team manager, told , the full consequences will take quite a while to sink in.Given the strength of the lineup in Monaco, when this year's Vuelta a España began on August 22, did you feel it would be very complicated to try and win it? No doubt about it. Anywhere where our friend Pogačar is racing, in the best of cases, a second place is what's possible. But at the same time, bad luck causes things to happen to us.It's also true that on the stage to Castelló, [where Mas caught Pogačar at the top of the main climb and they reached the finish together], that's where he showed us the first sign that he was in really great shape. Then the bad luck Tadej suffered meant Enric was converted into the overall leader, and from that day onwards, he knew how to keep the jersey all the way to here.And the fact that Mas had such a tough time in the Giro and then kicked off again from scratch, how much did that help him? We're never going to know how much that did, but we do know that after what happened to him in the 2025 Tour, he was almost four or five months without riding the bike. He had to start all over again this season, he went to the Giro and he was feeling great when he started, he was very optimistic. But probably his underlying physical condition was not in the right place where he wanted it to be, and he wasn't able to do the Giro how he wanted or expected.But he kept on training, and then you all saw that in Burgos he was already going well, and then here he was faultless. He followed the same progress curve as in other years, too, where the Vuelta and the months of August and September were his best months and then the end of the season, which is where he has his best results.That's what we're focused on now, and we don't know how the operation that he had because of the thrombophlebitis last year has helped him, too, in the long term. The important thing is that he feels very good and I think this series of results is helping him feel more and more confident and this is the final consequence. That's also come thanks to the team, who, despite the absence of Cian [Uijtdebroeks abandoned on stage 3 - Ed.] has done a great Vuelta.Quite a few people have been surprised that Enric has been able to handle the pressure of being the race leader, because we're talking about somebody who has had some issues with questions like descending and so on. Were you surprised as well?Yes. I was surprised as well. He was a rider who had a really promising start to his career and, when he was very young, even making second in the 2018 Vuelta, and the expectations that surrounded him were very high. He, too, was convinced that he could handle them, but in fact, he never could. I don't know that calendar we had for him of Tour-Vuelta-Tour-Vuelta-Tour-Vuelta etc. was … sometimes the Tour is really positive for a rider and sometimes it's a real burden of responsibility which some riders have problems overcoming and sometimes they never do. And he started to feel uncomfortable with that.But it's also true that he's a rider with a great future ahead of him, at least two or three years and above all, I think this Vuelta and the way he's raced through it will help consolidate his feelings of self-confidence.Old Rock'n'Rollers Never Die Was stage 20 maybe the most complicated of all to handle, with those early attacks that led to crosswinds, your support riders ahead of the GC group in breaks and Enric isolated in the main group for a large part of the toughest day of the race? Rather than being alone on the stage, we had riders ahead of him which we could use in the race when we thought it was necessary. He was alone for a while, but as I say, the directors played their cards very well strategically and when he needed riders, the team had them ready. And in that sense, I'm very, very satisfied with how teammates of his, who'd never had a chance to fight for a leader's jersey in a Grand Tour, rose to the occasion.What does this mean for a team and a country with a huge tradition in Grand Tours but which has struggled to get to the very top in the last few years. Is it a timely reminder that, as the Spanish song puts it, los viejos rockeros nunca mueren - old rock'n'rollers never die?Exactly. As you know very well, we're a team that has always had the concept of grandes corredores para las grandes vueltas - top-name riders for the biggest Tours - as one of our trademarks. That's been our reference point, ever since we started in 1980 but what has happened in the last few years, three riders - Roglič, Vingegaard and Pogačar - have won almost everything in the last six years. There's been virtually no space for anybody else. There've been a few isolated exceptions, but that's been it.What's happened is that with the internationalisation of cycling, we've got top-name riders from all over the world. But now we're benefiting from that expansion too, as a sport that's getting more and more popular across the globe. But I always think that the countries that have always been the cycling heartlands in Europe - Belgium, Spain, Italy and France - are always going to have top-name riders for Grand Tours, too.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. You'll get comprehensive race coverage of La Vuelta a España, subscriber-exclusive analysis from our expert columnists, in-depth features and industry-leading tech insight. Plus, the Cyclingnews app lets you follow the action wherever you go!

item.title: 'I was literally bleeding out' – Chris Froome goes into detail on the injuries that 'almost killed' him, and why he assumed everyone knew he'd retired
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: Chris Froome has for the first time described in detail the injuries he sustained in a training crash in August 2025, and addressed the confusion surrounding his retirement from the sport. Speaking to , the four-time Tour de France champion revealed that he "almost died" in the crash, and that he "almost took it as a given" that the general public knew he had retired. At the time of the incident, a 40-year-old Chris Froome was coming to the end of a career that had seen him dominate Grand Tours between 2013 and 2018. But before he could wave goodbye on his own terms, the training ride crash put a terrifying full-stop on his career and left him in hospital with life-threatening injuries. Given that, at the time of the incident, Froome was nearing the end of a five-year contract with Israel-Premier Tech, it was clear the crash might also end his career, though no official confirmation came until this year’s Tour de France, when Froome was asked about his status at a press event for Skoda."A journalist asked me, 'do you still have plans of racing?' And I was just like, 'listen, this is by no means a retirement announcement, but let me make it absolutely clear: no, no desire whatsoever to be riding my bike anymore. I'm just thankful to be alive right now," said Froome, who was speaking with at the weekend at an event hosted by Ekoï, the brand that supplies clothing and helmets to his old team, NSN Cycling."I almost killed myself on the bike, it was months' hospital time and medical issues, and having to take medication to try and get myself back to health again. It was really just trying to sort myself out, to be able to live a normal life again, I almost took it as a given that everyone knew I'd stopped. "I was literally in hospital, still, through January. I crashed in August. I was in no state to be making announcements or doing PR."I told people when I signed my contract, I said 'this will be my last contract', so I thought it was very clear to people, even though I crashed before I was able to do an official retirement announcement."'If the ambulance hadn't got there so quickly, I don't think I'd be here today'Though Froome made no comment on whether he would have been physically able to have carried on racing after sustaining such catastrophic injuries, the details are shocking, and some readers might find his description upsetting. "I almost died," Froome said, his tone reflecting the gravity of the situation. "My pericardium was open, my heart was exposed. I broke all my ribs, [they] imploded into my chest cavity. "So I've got metal plates on each of my ribs to hold the rib cage open again, because the whole rib cage like basically collapsed, and the ribs did a lot of damage to the right lung, and one of the ribs tore open the pericardium."So I was literally bleeding out. The ambulance got there within, I think seven, eight minutes of my crash, if they hadn't got there so quickly, I don't think I'd be here today. So I'm extremely, extremely lucky."One of Froome’s weekend duties with Ekoï was riding his bike, but it was a long while after his crash before he was able to get out again."I did get on the bike literally just for a spin, I think it was in December sometime, but I had an infection around some of the metal plates that they put on my ribs, and I had to go back into surgery again, and more tubes into my lungs," he said. "It was only really the end of January, February that I was kind of back into it again. Slowly, just socially now, just getting out, just to clear the head and get out with friends and have a have a good time on the bike."Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia.
