item.title: Edd Straw's 2026 Spanish Grand Prix F1 driver rankings
item.author: Edd Straw
item.content:encoded: The inaugural Formula 1 race at the Madring was no classic - but the Spanish Grand Prix weekend as a whole did seriously test the grid.Here's who passed with flying colours, and who was found wanting...- Put in a mighty qualifying lap to take an unexpected pole position in what McLaren is certain wasn't the fastest car.- Held onto the lead at the start despite the lower grip level in the pole position grid box compared to second place, and built a healthy lead in the early stages.- Would have won without the virtual safety car being perfectly-timed to cost him the lead as he was the fastest in race conditions.- The rear stepping out at the last corner cost him three tenths in Q3, and denied him a potential all-time great qualifying lap. That was down to him misjudging how much his mighty lap up to then impacted tyre condition, but shows he didn't deliver the maximum possible.- Couldn't get past Verstappen in the closing stages. But considering how difficult overtaking was for everyone and how difficult Verstappen is to pass generally, that's not something he could have done much about. Only bad luck cost him victory.- Recovered from an alarming moment in La Monumental on his first Q2 run to put in a superb lap on his last run, "one of the best I've done", to top the midfield and reach Q3, outpacing team-mate Pierre Gasly.- Achieved the best-possible qualifying position for an Alpine by defeating Arvid Lindblad in Q3.- Drove a strong race to head the midfield pack, and overachieved by one place by holding off Oscar Piastri.- Left a fraction on the table in Q3 and was the driver with the biggest deficit to his theoretical best lap at 0.204s. Not that it made any difference to his position.- Had he been able to pass Gabriel Bortoleto, then Liam Lawson was beatable but given the overtaking challenge that's not a big negative. Probably his best through-weekend execution in F1. 13th 11th- Put in a good qualifying effort on his final Q2 lap, with the three-tenths gap to Bortoleto suggesting that in qualifying conditions the Haas wasn't quite at the level of the Audi.- Made a characteristically good start and jumped to 11th ahead of the Audis, which put him 10th once Lewis Hamilton retired early.- But for losing a place to Nico Hulkenberg in the VSC pitstops due to Haas's pit equipment not being as advanced as Audi's, he would almost certainly have scored a point.- Ollie Bearman's self-inflicted absence from qualifying and poor grid position make comparisons difficult, but there's nothing to suggest Ocon was leaving any significant laptime on the table.A well-executed weekend that merited a points finish in probably the eighth-best car.- While the Red Bull was stronger in qualifying conditions than on race pace, he got close to the maximum out of the car on Saturday - even if, as for most, there was maybe a little left on the table.- Even on a track where passing is difficult, did a good job to keep Norris behind.- While luck assisted him in the path to second, even if he'd stayed in third without jumping Norris it would have probably been about as much as was possible.- Given the first-corner move was always likely to lead to a chicane cut, you can argue that this led to him being behind Antonelli, who was the other beneficiary of Verstappen having to let Hamilton past. Largely made the most of the Red Bull.- Was clearly the faster Mercedes driver, with his pace advantage over George Russell clear-cut.- The vast majority of his race was well-executed, showing patience when holding position while long-running Leclerc led.- Needed luck on his side to win, as this gave him track position over Verstappen and Norris.- The frenetic first lap featured track cuts at Turn 1 and Turn 5, which led to him being shuffled back to third.No question about his pace, but a little untidiness.- Despite the self-inflicted disadvantage of having to run some old-spec power unit components as a result of his Monza crash, he was just 0.005s down on Hamilton in qualifying.- Drove a good, clean race and did what he could in his lengthy hard stint, although ultimately the car pace meant that he was always likely to finish fourth once Hamilton had retired.- Probably left a little pace on the table in qualifying, particularly early in the lap owing to the prep laps not being perfectly executed, but as he put it, still delivered "quite a clean lap" albeit with "a few moments here and there". No major negatives, but still didn't look at his absolute best.- While the huge advantage over Valtteri Bottas was inflated by his team-mate being impeded by Carlos Sainz on his final lap, Perez always looked destined to be the faster Cadillac in qualifying. And he executed well, with a strong final lap.- Drove a strong race before a water leak in the power unit led to him first slowing then retiring, having gained places to the Turn 1 incident then chased Alex Albon.- The only real downside is that he didn't have the chance to run the second half of the race, which wasn't his fault.A strong weekend when he was the quicker Cadillac driver. 16th 15th- Recovered superbly from practice troubles and his FP3 mistake to put in a strong Q1 lap. Although the advantage over Sainz was infinitesimal at 0.005s, that was a big step forward.- Williams didn't have the pace to have done any better than 16th in qualifying, especially given Albon didn't have a fresh set of softs left for Q2.- Drove a good race in a car that didn't have the pace to do any better.- Struggled on Friday with deployment problems that put him on the back foot and well off Sainz's pace.- Clipping the wall early in FP3 cost him important running. A strong weekend, with the FP3 wall-clip the one negative. 17th 17th- Always looked like the faster Aston Martin driver throughout the weekend.- Was able to show the strength of the car in certain corners, which was offset by time lost on the straights.- Battled on to the finish despite deployment troubles and a front wing change after being hit by Sainz.- He was a tenth and a half off his personal best in sector three on his final lap, which was sufficient to swing the battle for Q2 with Albon against him.- Race problems meant he was compromised, losing significant race time.A decent weekend, but perhaps could have got the Aston Martin into Q2.- While qualifying wasn't maximised, it still represented a decent recovery after his FP3 off cost him his simulation.- Probably had the stronger underlying pace of the Ferrari drivers, although didn't make the most of it.- Crash in FP3 cost him half of that session and his qualifying simulation run, despite his best efforts to get back to the pits against the team's instructions.- Didn't make the most of qualifying with a small error early in the lap that cost him time.Had the pace to achieve more, but compromised Saturday then brake misfortune meant he didn't show it.- Showed strong pace on Friday before his crash, but despite admitting to still being down on confidence in qualifying he made Q3.- Ran ahead of Piastri in the first stint after jumping him on the opening lap.- Managed to hold off Hulkenberg late on.- FP2 crash at Turn 13 when the rear end gave up immediately on turn-in cost him some running on a day when he was quick, with a hangover that led to him not joining FP3 until the closing stages.- Couldn't hold Piastri off after the McLaren driver had made his pitstop, but considering the advantage of fresh mediums there's no disgrace in that. FP2 crash had significant consequences, but Lindblad recovered well.11th 10th- Won the battle of imperfect execution with his team-mate in Q2 by 0.165s.- Made the most of starting on softs and the timing of the VSC to take a point.- Was the slightly better Audi driver when everything is taken into account.- There might have been a way to get past Lindblad late on, but hardly a big negative considering the difficulty of passing.- Didn't make the most of the car in qualifying, as slipping into Q3 was possible.A solid weekend's work, putting the Audi broadly where it should have been.- Made an important pass on Colapinto early on, albeit having lost the place at the start.- Stayed out on hards under the VSC, and made that strategy work decently to capitalise on Bortoleto holding up Colapinto to finish ahead of him.- Again struggled to follow Verstappen's pace steps as qualifying progressed, ending up a respectable but disappointed 0.352s down.- With the caveat that it's only his third outing in the Red Bull, he was very much in the group of top-team second drivers as defined by pace.Solid but unspectacular, with an unobtrusively effective race drive.- Was one of the few drivers to make a successful overtaking move by passing Lawson after he made his second pitstop.- Had a clean weekend and was on the wrong side of the VSC in terms of having started on the hard tyres - although that was a deliberate choice to open up the possibility of staying out if there was an early interruption. This was closed off when Leclerc ahead did the same thing, leading to Russell stopping and then, thanks to the mediums not having the range, having to make a second pitstop.- There was no hint of him being at Antonelli's level throughout the weekend.- Asked a little too much of the tyres at Turn 11 on his final Q3 lap, which cost him time but he was already gradually slipping back from Antonelli prior to that.A step back from Antonelli in terms of pace.- Wasn't at fault for the front-wing damage on the opening lap that compromised his race.- Managed to pass Lindblad after making his pitstop, having run the hard/medium strategy without a VSC stop.- Simply wasn't at Norris's level in terms of pace.- Couldn't find a way past Colapinto in the closing stages. A lacklustre weekend. 12th 13th- Drove a tidy long stint on hards, keeping the quicker Colapinto behind him.- Was unlucky with the VSC timing given he had started on hards.- Wasn't at his best in qualifying, admitting he didn't extract the maximum from the car with being a little too conservative into Turn 1 putting him on the back foot versus Hulkenberg.- Poor start dropped him down to 15th, but that's mitigated by the fact he was on hard Pirellis.A middling weekend, marginally worse than Hulkenberg's.14th 12th- Showed good pace in the race, but the timing of the VSC meant he stayed out on hards and that didn't allow him to translate it into points.- His underlying speed was, save for when it really mattered in qualifying, where you'd expect it to be.- Lacklustre in qualifying, expressing bafflement at a car that felt good in FP3 struggling for grip in qualifying thanks to poor tyre prep on the outlap.- Picked up a five-second penalty added at the end of the race for speeding in the pits, which was needless although it only cost him time, not a position.Poor qualifying defined his weekend.19th 18th- The 2.098s qualifying deficit to Perez was completely unrepresentative because Bottas had to rely on his first-run time, with the second ruined by traffic and the third by Sainz impeding him.- Looked the slower Cadillac driver overall.- Race gave him little opportunity to shine given the damage he picked up through no fault of his own. Had bad luck in both qualifying and the race, but didn't look to be at Perez's level.- Ran ahead of Alonso for a couple of laps early on before falling behind him approaching Turn 13.- Brake troubles and damage from debris meant that the race comparison with Alonso doesn't mean anything.- Had no opportunity in qualifying given a water leak prevented him setting a time in Q1, but there was nothing before that to suggest he would have been close to Alonso's pace.- Single-lap pace ultimately wasn't a factor for Stroll given he had a 40-place grid penalty for power-unit element changes, which limited his opportunities to impress. That context significantly mitigates the negative of the fact he didn't show anything like Alonso's single-lap pace through practice.No chance in qualifying or the race, but also no glimmers of Alonso-like pace elsewhere.15th 14th- Considering the damage, his race pace was respectable, but losing time behind Perez early on limited his horizons.- Struggled in qualifying, with the 0.880s deficit to Lindblad down to Tsunoda being far happier with the car on scrubbed tyres than fresh ones. This meant he couldn't exploit the peak of the available grip and was therefore nowhere.- Damage at the first corner from being clobbered by Sainz meant there was no opportunity to recover from a difficult qualifying. A nothing weekend thanks to qualifying struggles and race damage.- Showed good pace on Friday and seemed on form heading into qualifying.- While the pitwall takes the responsibility for being oblivious to Bottas's presence and not warning Sainz, the driver always has to take a small share of the blame, even with visibility limited.- Qualified behind Albon (by 0.005s) but pointed to poor timing of the final run and a straightline deficit as holding him back.- Was caught out by the inevitable Turn 1 concertina at the start then compromised his race by hitting Alonso.Pace was fine, but too many errors. 22nd (pits) 16th- Drove a good race from the pitlane, although his two on-track passes were of the damaged Bottas and Stroll.- Crashing heavily in FP3 after tagging the inside wall in the Turn 10/11 sweep caused a major accident - and came after a warning on Friday when he clipped the front-left at Turn 15 with less serious consequences. It also cost him qualifying. As he said, "I have only myself to blame" for the shunt that defined his weekend.

item.title: San Marino Grand Prix MotoGP rider rankings 2026
item.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
item.content:encoded: The San Marino Grand Prix weekend at Misano was dominated by Spaniards - and so are our MotoGP rider rankings for the weekend. But which of the two clear standouts leads the way this time? 2nd 1st 1stFor the second weekend running the 2027 Ducati line-up monopolises the top two in these rankings - and this time Marquez gets the nod, again by the narrowest of margins.He had claimed on Friday he would "sign right now" for a podium and that Marco Bezzecchi was the favourite - and whether that was 'mind games-y' or not, the claim did seem backed up by what was going on on track.But a bet on the medium rear combined with another great approach to Turn 1 at the start won Marquez the sprint - and he controlled the main race after Bezzecchi's exit.At a track which doles out a real punishment to the right side of the body - where Marquez is compromised - he was the top Ducati in every session. 7th 6th 3rdThe standards remain sky high for Acosta, who got his customary Friday crash out of the way early on and subsequently was again on another level compared to his fellow KTM riders.He lamented losing ground in a Fermin Aldeguer battle in the sprint - in which he claimed both were doing "stupid s**t" - and was generally unhappy with the stopping performance of his RC16.But a "disaster"-esque warm-up on Sunday was followed up by a fantastic ride in the grand prix, delivering another podium that had never felt on the cards for KTM. 3rd8th 4thAldeguer had a technical issue on Friday that cost him a real shot at Q2, so did it the hard way on Saturday morning - powering to third on the grid in one of his best qualifying efforts yet in MotoGP.He got roughed up a bit on the sprint, by Acosta but particularly by Raul Fernandez, and then coped much better in the main race with the field more spread out and the pace clearly strong.Given Misano is so demanding physically, and Aldeguer is still injury-limited (and also riding an old bike), this was a triumph of a weekend.6th 9th 9thMarini's best weekend of the year, the high point of it a Q2 run to a spectacular sixth on the grid - which he did admit was probably aided by yellow-flag timings and others messing up.Never one for excessive modesty, he described himself as "every time faster than my team-mates" this weekend - and the two races bore that out.He was "giving everything" on Sunday to keep Fabio Di Giannantonio at bay - laughing that "for sure he hates me!" given the defensive lines, though Di Giannantonio saw no issue with it and was full of praise for his friend. Ultimately, that defensive effort was for naught, a late-race vibration in the rear forcing Marini to simply drag the bike to the finish.9th 5th 2ndSuper-fast again, the younger Marquez had performance for a front-row start and should have been in the mix to snipe a win.A two-crash Q2, in which he was wrong-footed by adjusting to a new soft tyre after running used rubber in preceding practice, was a hammer blow to his hopes of a truly amazing result.Still, he recovered well in both races, so well that many went away after Sunday's contest wondering whether he really should have worked his way past his brother and put himself in position to win. 5th3rd 5thThis was so nearly an almighty smash-and-grab by Martin, who went from trailing Aprilia team-mate Bezzecchi by six tenths of a second in qualifying to being in position to win the race and extend his championship lead.Whether he would've won the race without his compartment syndrome issue is conjecture at this point - but he certainly he feels he could have, and he feels that his title charge is emboldened by this weekend, as long as he can suitably address this arm issue, through surgery or management.There is still a very substantial single-lap question mark - 0.546s off on Friday, 0.587s off on Saturday is a losing formula - but there's something to be said for how deftly he was navigating the race circumstances this weekend.4th 4th 7thDi Giannantonio was pacing for a front row (or maybe even better) after three corners of his final Q2 lap, then went down in Turn 4.But it didn't compromise his grid position too much, and that anyway didn't seem all that important to the outcome of his weekend.Much more impactful was that early grand prix melee that dropped him into the mid-pack - with Aldeguer squeezing him to the outside kerb at Turn 1 in the inciting incident - and a subsequent brake-lever concern that limited his ability to overtake back up the order. 13th 21st 10thMake no mistake - after the unseemly business of his stroppy back-and-forth with Yamaha at Aragon, Quartararo properly showed up at Misano.That was easy to overlook given his most notable moment of the weekend was a clumsy fall on the sprint while trying to set up a move on Diogo Moreira - but this indirectly will have been a consequence of being the only Yamaha rider with the potential to do anything of note. Of the 11 1m31s laps delivered by Yamahas in the sprint, Quartararo was responsible for all 11."It's clear he has more than us this weekend," admitted team-mate Alex Rins, usually not one to acknowledge it so plainly.Quartararo's grand prix was more muted in terms of performance, due to a need to conserve fuel - but given that he stood his ground impressively in the top 10.10th 7th 6thFernandez wasn't perfect, but clearly wasn't given the best opportunities to make much of this weekend. A return of seventh and sixth in the two races is kind of the bare minimum given the level of the Aprilia, but he can't really be faulted.He did labour a bit on Friday, with errors in crucial moments, but navigated Q1 well - including a massive "one in 15" save tucking the front at Turn 1. But in Q2 there was a "problem on both bikes", so he was well off his Q1 time and grid position-limited, conditioning both races.An unexpected fuel-consumption problem on Sunday meant he was in the lean engine map for virtually the whole thing and never got the chance to pick off the arm-pump-limited Martin or show much of anything.16th15th 8thBastianini just missed out on Friday on what would have been a weekend-transforming top-10 place. He had decided against fitting a fresh front tyre for his final time attack - which is not an unconventional decision, but in his case it proved "a big mistake".The pace was probably there to do better (he set his fastest lap of the grand prix, and a very good one at that, on the final lap, in typical Bastianini fashion) but from 16th on the grid it was never really on the cards, and even for all these caveats there is little doubt the transcendent Acosta had much more performance.12th 16th 14th'The world's fastest journalist', or whatever they say, lived up to the billing this weekend by grabbing onto the back of Acosta and powering to a great Q2 appearance.But that 'journalist' quip is increasingly more relevant. It has been a long, long while since Espargaro has raced regularly and it is showing. He "missed the aggression to overtake" on Saturday, and Sunday's race exhausted him.He was all too keenly aware at the end that he was a 35-year-old fighting against a grid of largely 20-somethings. "My respect to Marc Marquez and Johann Zarco!" he laughed.21st 18th 12thThe best laptime of Razgatlioglu's weekend came in the grand prix, on lap 12. If you know your MotoGP, you know this is extremely suboptimal in terms of extracting a positive result.He said knowledge of Misano from World Superbike "did not help" here, and his one-lap pace was extremely poor, particularly in a "very bad" Q1.But the race pace was obviously there, at a fairly high level. He was the top Yamaha on the road, in the sprint, though lost a position for track limits, then was right with Yamaha benchmark Quartararo in the grand prix - though again fell foul of track limits, even if the resulting long lap didn't actually cost him a position.11th 10th DNFThe follow-up at Misano was more like what we all would have expected from Zarco's comeback weekend at Aragon - and even so, the actual speed was fairly decent.Zarco navigated Friday well to land in Q2, but this was probably flattering his ultimate potential race trim. Still, he could have been much higher on the grid had he improved on his second Q2 run - and had he avoided a penalty for impeding Bezzecchi, which he acknowledged as "totally fair".He got stuck behind a fuel-managing Quartararo on Sunday before missing his braking at Turn 8 late on and going down.17th 20th DNFMir was markedly slower than usual relative to his fellow Honda riders, but this seemed to have less to do with a lack of confidence on braking he reported on Friday and more to do with some sort of unspecified ailment that increasingly bothered him over the weekend.Suffering from a headache and with no strength, he gutted it through a fruitless sprint but had to give up very early in the main race, fearing that riding around "would only make the situation worse".He now has medical tests to do between here and the Red Bull Ring to properly figure out his situation.15th11th DNFAfter a run of really strong form of late, Misano was largely a letdown for Moreira.For most of the weekend, the third sector - and Curvone in particular - was the culprit, as he and LCR struggled to stabilise the Honda sufficiently in the fast right-hander.He said after the sprint: "I told Honda, tomorrow we're cutting this corner, I don't care!" But Moreira actually made a bit of a breakthrough there in Sunday warm-up, then fell off right away on Sunday without managing to properly confirm his work. 1st 2nd DNFThis one will sting for a while.A 37-point weekend looked on the cards for Bezzecchi after his blistering record lap in Q2 - but it turned into a nine-pointer instead, with defeat in the sprint and catastrophe in the main race.He seemed in a real hurry to break away from Marquez and the rest of them at the start of the grand prix, but with the bike unsettled through Curvone and the subsequent Turn 12 he arrived at Turn 13 compromised and lost the front.Forget about this being a home race or whatever. This is a monumental blow for his championship. 19th14th 11th"Not fast enough" was Binder's summary through the weekend and at the end of it. His qualifying was "a bit s**t" and his race pace was generally underwhelming, but he did spare his KTM team any repair bills and finished in the points.He's pacing for an inglorious, ill-fitting conclusion to his MotoGP tenure - but is at least just quietly struggling rather than properly imploding. Or is it better to burn out than to fade away (my my, hey hey)? 8th 12th 13thDespite lacking confidence again with the Ducati GP25, Morbidelli looked notably more competitive than for most of his difficult final season in MotoGP. He gets a bit of credit for this - but it gets almost entirely offset by the fact he didn't capitalise on the opportunity.Another instance of impeding a fellow rider - this time Bastianini on Friday - needlessly capped his Sunday potential by virtue of a long lap penalty, meaning Saturday was the best shot at a headline result.But no such luck. He looked uncharacteristically timid in the early laps of the sprint, roughed up a bit by Moreira and then forced to spend the rest of the race shadowing the LCR Honda rider without a way past. 20th 19th DNFFriday had looked gently encouraging but proved a mirage as Rins ultimately just didn't have all that much performance to offer this weekend - and was not happy with the bike.He was only ever in play for some attrition-aided points on Sunday but became part of said attrition, parking up as he suffered from a "migraine and severe nausea".18th17th DNFA freak "cold brakes, cold tyres" crash at Rio literally something like 30 seconds into the weekend set the tone for Miller.He just wasn't very competitive, chasing the right set-up all throughout and falling off in the grand prix as early as lap two shortly after a ding-dong battle with Zarco.He said the bike felt improved on Sunday but "I didn't get to do bugger all on it".14th13thDNFFavourable track, unfavourable track, home track, foreign track, left-handers, right-handers, hard braking, high-speed - suddenly it just doesn't seem to matter at all.This is the third time in a row (and yet only the third time this season) that Bagnaia sits lower than 20th in these rankings. He has looked all wrong since his arm-pump surgery - though he clearly seems of the opinion this is more coincidence than causation."It's extremely easy to see the difference between what my bike is doing compared to all the other Ducatis. Big, big difference, but difficult to understand why," Bagnaia lamented in-weekend, hitting a familiar note. He could not extract rear grip and struggled to stay on the bike, feeling "humiliated" by the experience.The Turn 2 crash in the grand prix delivered a coup de grace to this terrible weekend - but who's to say it will be any better in Austria?

item.title: 'I expect a very hard race with big time gaps' – A UCI Gravel World Championships title defence for Florian Vermeersch in Nannup
item.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
item.content:encoded: The winner of the 2025 UCI Gravel World Championships elite men's race, Florian Vermeersch, has decided to make the trip out to Australia to defend his world title on the gravel roads of Nannup.The Belgian UAE Team Emirates-XRG rider won the title in the Netherlands with a solo effort of nearly 20km on the 180km course with 1,650 metres of climbing, with the victory finally coming after two years of taking the runner up slot at the event. This year he'll be lining up in prime position on Sunday October 11 and with the number one on his back on a decidedly different course, and one which is also considerably further from home. The race in the remote location of Nannup will unfold over one lap of a 140.7km loop that is heavy on gravel and also throws in 3,625m of elevation gain across a series of climbs. "Going to the Worlds as defending champion is a special feeling, but it doesn't put any extra pressure on me. I just love to do gravel races and when it fits my calendar. I'm always in," said Vermeersch in a release from the Australian race organisers."It would be awesome to be the first two-time winner but I'm aware that it’s not going to be easy. There are very strong competitors on the starting line."The course looks very hard and demanding so I expect a very hard race with big time gaps."Vermeersch is one of the riders in the field that spends the vast majority of his time on the road, though he did give the jersey of the gravel world champion an outing at the Marly Gravel race in May, where he finished fourth in the race won by Wout van Aert (Visma-Lease a Bike).This time Vermeersch will be lining up against some key gravel specialists, who were absent last year, with South Africa's Matt Beers and Keegan Swenson set to be on the start line. Their Specialized Off-road teammate – as well as The Traka 360, Unbound 200 and European Championships winner – Mads Würtz Schmidt will also be another key favourite on the start line.The confirmed entries so far for the elite women's race on Saturday October 10 are also setting up a charged battle between the gravel specialists and riders crossing the discipline boundaries. The Dutch multi-discipline master of Marianne Vos (Visma-Lease a Bike), who won the gravel world title in 2024, is among the confirmed starters, as is the dominant figure in the un-sanctioned world of gravel, Sofia Gomez Villafañe (Specialized Off-road).Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: Everything we learned from F1's 2026 Spanish Grand Prix
item.author: Matt Beer
item.content:encoded: But that's not to say the weekend was a dud: the track proved a hit with drivers, and away from it there were significant revelations - about this year's title fight, but also involving the bid to keep one of F1's star drivers in the championship.Here are our main takeaways from the Madring: Hamilton's title bid is overYou may not have felt like there was a realistic Lewis Hamilton/Ferrari 2026 F1 title bid ongoing for a while (or, if you're sceptical, ever) but there was a notable change in tone from Hamilton about it after his early retirement with brake problems in Madrid.In recent weeks his warnings to Ferrari over its management of races and its drivers had been all about how the title shot was getting more distant at best.But when Sky Sports F1 put it to him in Madrid that Kimi Antonelli "looks hard to stop now", Hamilton pretty much congratulated his Mercedes replacement on the 2026 title."There's no stopping him and Mercedes this year," said Hamilton. "I think they've done a phenomenal job and they deserve it."Which was about two steps further down that road than he really needed to go in the circumstances. The fact Hamilton went there shows that - at least in the immediate disgruntlement of his early Madrid retirement - the last title hope is now gone in his mind.With the deficit now up to 101 points and few signs lately of Ferrari having Mercedes-beating pace, it would be hard to imagine any other scenario.Aston Martin really needs some Honda helpIt emerged at the Madring that FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has been speaking to Fernando Alonso and Aston Martin owner Lawrence Stroll about the prospect of giving Honda some extra help to boost its recovery plan.The Madring weekend exposed yet again that Honda is lacking - even though it is a far less power-sensitive circuit than Monza.Alonso said "the engine was very bad today" after the race, saying he almost stalled at the pitstops because of an engine issue. He also reported the power unit was struggling to recover when he was slowing to respect blue flags.So a boost for Honda can't come soon enough, and we know there isn't another major Honda upgrade coming until 2027.Any such extra help - be it homologation freedoms, extra spending allowances, or specific rule changes in areas where Honda is failing to make progress - will require the support of other power unit manufacturers.The good thing for Aston Martin Honda is that both Mercedes and Red Bull were receptive to the idea of once again assisting Honda, as its rivals did earlier this year.Exactly how, what they may leverage in return, and where everyone stands in private, remains to be seen.But the Madring was a stark reminder of how welcome that help would be right now.Red Bull's car is still degradingThe mysterious 'car degradation' problems afflicting Red Bull this season aren't going away, based on both Max Verstappen and team principal Laurent Mekies' comments in Madrid.Red Bull is still not offering any insight on precisely what the problem is, but Mekies admitted it's still there, has been for a long time, and will be for the rest of the season."There is an element of car performance degradation that is happening through a session and through a race," said Mekies."He's [Verstappen is] right in saying it's not a new issue. We are not sleeping on it. We have been trying to tackle that in different ways."Obviously, I consider it a complex issue, otherwise we would get to the bottom of it. But everyone is very constructive about it and tries to make small steps at the time to be able to get to the bottom of it eventually."We had a couple of positive steps in that regard this weekend. It will never be the full picture, but we certainly have - through pain - made progress in our understanding."We don't have all the solutions yet in the car, but I trust that we are on the right way. It will not be fast, so it's something that will probably take us through next year."This wasn't the ideal Madring layoutAs you may have seen, The Race revealed on Monday that three key areas of the track have been identified for improvement to increase the prospect of overtaking after a race bereft of passing.What we've also learned is that those revisions - to the Turn 5 braking zone at the end of the first sector, the Turn 13 left-hander after La Monumental, and the tight Turn 20 - had already been proposed to the FIA before this year's race.That they weren't implemented for its F1 debut, and are being made for 2027 instead, comes down to two factors: the complexities of track simulations, and complicated homologation processes.The construction of the Madring was already tight, time-wise - work started in April last year - and was delayed by a wet winter in Madrid.So, the safer option was to avoid any changes so no extra delays were built into the homologation process that could've hindered the construction work and opened the door to much bigger issues had the track not been ready in time.In the case of the Madring, that process also required the involvement of local authorities. Consider that road, rail, and aviation stakeholders all needed to be consulted, alongside emergency officials and water, drainage, and other environmental agencies, and you can see why this was a risk-averse first race on this 'street' circuit.But expect the Madring to look a little different when F1 returns next Autumn.This isn't the end of Williams's 2026 painWilliams awaits its big 2026 upgrade at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix but Alex Albon doesn’t think it will be enough to turn the team into a midfield contender.Albon had another frustrating race in Madrid where he probably maximised the package, but still finished 15th, while Carlos Sainz retired with damage.Albon said he was "just waiting for Baku" - but changed his tone when asked by The Race's Edd Straw what he was expecting from the step."We're finishing, really simply, 50 seconds behind the midfield at the minute in the race - so we're losing a second a lap more or less in the race, and it needs to be a pretty big upgrade to do it [wipe out that gap]," he said."All we know, it's going to be a good step, but is it going to be the full step? I'm hopeful for it, but I don't think it would be."Unfortunately, we said it last year, but the focus is on next year as well, and we realise we're too far back at the moment to have a couple of upgrades for this year. We need to focus on next year."He added that the rate of development among the midfield has seen some teams bring "three or four upgrades a year" recently, and said some of those upgrades are "huge".Alpine made a big step back to the front of that pack with its Dutch GP package, and Haas made progress with its Monza upgrade - and both teams are already in front of Williams.Albon explained: "If you think of us in a normal year, Baku would have put us back in contention, but we have to be honest with ourselves, the speed of the development race this year is huge, and we've fallen back."It is therefore unlikely that Williams will contend for points in Azerbaijan and add to its tally of 11 - but previous editions of that race have proven chaotic.Gasly's Monza pole catalysed ColapintoThe elation from Pierre Gasly's pole position at Monza might have been short-lived given he was quickly consumed by faster rivals in the race, but that Saturday result did prove useful for Alpine team-mate Franco Colapinto.At Madrid, Colapinto qualified ninth and finished seventh ahead of McLaren's Oscar Piastri, with another great start off the line.He was particularly pleased with his execution of the Madrid weekend - and credited it to learnings gained from Gasly's Monza pole."After Monza, I learned a lot of the quali of Pierre and I tried to do a step here. And I did it. And I maximised everything again," he said, when asked by The Race's Edd Straw whether this was his best F1 weekend in terms of execution."The quali was one of the best I've done. With very, very, very perfect laps. And putting the car in Q3 - that was always a bit tricky with the Audis going very fast here. And today, we stayed in front in the race and scored a lot of points."So, very happy. Again, it's extremely positive. And I'm very happy with the pace and the results."He explained that Gasly's experience gave him useful information "on everything" in terms of qualifying execution in Madrid."On driving and energy management, from run to run, from Q1 to Q2 to Q3, were very clear. And yeah, I learned from that."Here, I was really on it in qualifying. On a very difficult track. Probably the most difficult one of the year to nail a lap. And also the most satisfying one when you do it. And both Q2 and Q3 were amazing laps."It's happy days at Alpine, with Gasly - who was 12th after waiting until the end of the race to pit - also buoyed for Baku."Honestly, the pace was insane after that VSC [virtual safety car]. I think it's really positive," he claimed.Haas is close to ending points droughtHaas hasn't scored a point since the Monaco GP in early June, but it did come very close to ending that dry spell in Madrid.The car inconsistency issues that have plagued Haas all season weren't present here and Esteban Ocon was running 10th in the early stages.But he was then jumped in the pitlane under the virtual safety car by Nico Hulkenberg because of an Audi pitstop that, in terms of time spent in the pitlane, was 1.133s faster than Haas's."We lost out on the pitstop against Audi, but I don't believe it was our team's fault; it's really the equipment that we need to improve to give them a better chance," Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu explained.That dropped Ocon just out of the net points-paying positions, leaving him 11th at the chequered flag despite a late push.But Ocon still felt that was an overachievement, saying "we extracted more than what the car could do" even if he was "sad at the same time because we could have got a point".Team-mate Ollie Bearman couldn't do the same after the FP3 crash that ensured he missed qualifying, started from the pitlane and ended up 16th.But Bearman thinks Baku will suit the upgraded Haas as it hopes to fend off an Audi team that's been slowly chipping away at Haas's points advantage in the fight for seventh in the constructors' championship.

item.title: The London hospital funded by donors who invested in the slave trade
item.author: Written by Morgan Ofori and David Conn; Animation by Alexander Purcell; Photography by Wayne Crichlow
item.content:encoded: Barts is one of many UK institutions whose benefactors were involved in the trafficking of enslaved AfricansInside the Great Hall of St Bartholomew’s North Wing, alongside stately portraits of the apostle from whom London’s oldest hospital takes its name and King Henry VIII, extravagant commemorative boards adorn the walls.The Great Hall was a grand, formal space where governors weighed their philanthropic donations and drafted their wills, many while investing in the stock of companies built on the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Today, many of those donors are commemorated in acrylic gold paint on the boards.Continue reading...

item.content:encoded: Public offering of Aliko Dangote’s Nigerian oil refinery business could swell his net wealth by two-thirdsThe fortune of Africa’s richest person could swell by two thirds to nearly $60bn (£44bn) after his refinery in Nigeria listed publicly in the continent’s biggest-ever initial public offering.If Monday’s flotation of Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals on the Nigerian exchange goes to plan, then Aliko Dangote will add a further $23bn (£17bn) to his $35bn net worth.Continue reading...

item.title: 'I think I took last year for granted' – Oscar Onley fights through setbacks with vital lessons learnt from successful rollercoaster Vuelta a España
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: Three weeks, two crashes, and one stomach bug later, Oscar Onley arrived at the finale of his first Grand Tour with Netcompany Ineos in Granada with some important lessons learned, taking sixth overall and the white jersey of Best Young Rider at the Vuelta a España after a rollercoaster race. But it all threatened to come unstuck before he really got going at his second Vuelta, with the fourth stage to Andorra making him consider whether it was worth continuing on, having suffered stomach issues overnight.It wasn't an easy road, but with a mixture of successes and failures across the 21 stages, Onley agreed that his fourth Grand Tour had had a bit of everything. "That sums up pretty well. I think when I look back at where I was with the setbacks I had throughout the first two weeks, especially, then actually to still be in that GC position by the end was something I'm quite proud of," said the young Scot, speaking to after the final podium ceremony on Sunday evening. "Especially on that Andorra stage, I got quite sick overnight, and I was really expecting to – to be honest, I was half expecting to turn off the course halfway through and ride home because, yeah, I was pretty down bad that morning, but so I'm quite happy overall."Joining Ineos as a headline signing for 2026, Onley arrived as a big-money transfer, fresh off the back of finishing fourth at the Tour de France, and with a lot of pressure on his shoulders. He was expected to be a main leader, but struggled throughout the season with setback after setback stunting his development.Thinking back to that Tour, in comparison to the tough road he's endured this Vuelta, Onley had gained some perspective. This gritty performance and 2026 season could prove to be more useful for his career, in the way he's had to handle the setbacks and comebacks."I think I took last year for granted," he said honestly, "Like I literally had no setbacks or nothing went wrong in that Tour. I think what I experienced in this Grand Tour is more probably more normal, I would say. Everyone has setbacks during a Grand Tour, and it's kind of about how you deal with them. "The team have been really, really calm around it, and we've really made good plans on how to recover from these setbacks, especially that second crash. Initially, I didn't think it set me back much, but actually, my body didn't really react in the way I wanted it to, and it took quite a few days to really recover from that. "So we kind of went into quite conservative mode and really tried to make the most of that, and it made a big difference when it came to well. The first goal was the TT after that, so yeah, it shows that it works."Learning from the experience of Jack HaigOne of the key members of the roster who guided him was former Vuelta podium finisher Jack Haig, whose experience offered a calm shoulder for Onley to lean on, both in hectic finishes and in the mountains. In what was just their first race together, it wouldn't be surprising to see the Scot request the services of the Australian as he develops further as Netcompany Ineos' main GC rider. "This was my first race with Jack, so that was also something that I wasn't sure how it would go in the beginning because obviously, to start a Grand Tour with riders you've not actually raced with is something quite unique," Onley told . "But I feel like we, not just Jack, but the whole team in general, clicked straight away. I think from stage 2 on we were really on it, and Jack especially is someone that has been in my position going for GC before, so he understands my thoughts and how I'm feeling towards certain situations. "I feel I was following his wheel quite a lot on the flatter days, actually, in the finals, and it made me calmer because you know he's someone that's not going to take risks and yeah he's taking it in the smoothest way, which definitely made me feel more relaxed about everything."While Onley dropped out of the top five spot he was occupying before the final mountain stage to Collado del Alguacil on Saturday, with a long-range Sepp Kuss (Visma-Lease a Bike) raid jumping him up six spots from eleventh, after the season he's had it should prove an important performance in his career. The stage to Alto de Aitana on stage 9 was perhaps the best version of Onley we saw at this Vuelta, finishing second there behind overall winner Enric Mas, but with a more consistent run into racing in 2027, he can expect to aim much higher and back to the levels he performed at during last year's Tour. His next race won't be in the stage racing arena, however, as for the first time this season he will be taking on a one-day race at the UCI Road World Championships in Montreal, set to play a supporting role for Tom Pidcock and Adam Yates. item.title: After tough season, Ben Healy finds rhythm and form in time for World Championships
item.author: Matilda Price
item.content:encoded: After a mixed bag of a season that saw him miss the Spring Classics and hunt for form at the Tour de France, Ben Healy seems to be finding his legs just in time for the World Championships, with a strong ride at the Grand Prix de Montréal.Healy had an unforgettable 2025 season, winning a stage of the Tour and spending a stint in the yellow jersey before finishing third in the World Championships road race in Kigali, but has struggled to climb to those heights again in 2026.Before Sunday, he hadn't finished in the top 10 of a race since March, but a big breakaway effort at the GP de Montréal and a strong ride after he was caught saw him take eighth on the course that will host the World Championships in two weeks' time."It was super hard," a tired Healy told at the end of the race, having spent 52km out front."I think it's known as one of the hardest of the year, this race, so it's nice. I was feeling good, I gave it a go. Not to be today, but the big one is in a couple of weeks."As well as clearly refinding his own strength after a bit of a reset over the summer, Healy's strong Sunday was helped by the efforts of his team. With teammate Michael Leonard up the road with Juan Ayuso (Lidl-Trek) in an earlier break, the Irishman saw an opportunity to capitalise on his good legs. "We just always wanted to be on the front foot today, and put guys up the road, and it just gives you that option if you want to take it," he said. "I could see Michael was strong, and it wasn't really the plan, but you know, when you race like that, you give yourself options, and I used that option today."Though he was ultimately disappointed to not be able to convert his long escape into a stronger effort, Healy could say positives that his legs are good and his level is "there or thereabouts" compared to his competitors heading into this final part of the season. "Yeah, 100%," he said when asked if he felt his form was returning at just the right moment. "I was feeling really good today, so I'm in the right place. I know the preparation's there, and the Worlds type of racing really suits me, so yeah, I'm ready."Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: 'The right time to take a different path' – Blanka Vas engineers early exit from SD Worx-Protime
item.author: Patrick Fletcher
item.content:encoded: There has been another shock move in the women’s transfer market, with the Hungarian champion Blanka Vas to make a mid-season switch from SD Worx-Protime to Lidl-Trek. With a background in cyclocross and mountain bike, Vas had been marked out for greatness ever since joining the Women’s WorldTour with SD Worx mid-way through 2021. However, after seeing her career take off with wins in the Tour de France Femmes and Giro d’Italia Women, among other major races, her 2026 season has been one to forget, featuring just 12 race days, and no racing since May. On Monday morning, it was revealed in a coordinated announcement between SD Worx-Protime and Lidl-Trek that the 25-year-old would be making the switch between the teams, effective not from next January but from October 1, 2026. Mid-contract switches are not unheard of for riders who race cyclocross in the winter, but while Shirin van Anrooij is leaving Lidl-Trek to join Canyon-SRAM from November 1, Blanka Vas’ transfer comes with the possibility of the Hungarian champion representing her new team on the road this calendar year, as well as in cyclocross."Following open and constructive discussions, both parties have concluded that the sporting ambitions they had hoped for have not been realised over the past year. The decision has therefore been taken to give Vas the opportunity to start a new chapter in her career,” read a statement from SD Worx-Protime. The team indicated that the driving force for the parting of ways was Vas herself, with sporting director Danny Stam adding: “She has expressed a desire to explore what she can achieve with another team. We understand her position and wish her every success and happiness for the future."Soon after, Lidl-Trek announced the arrival of Vas from October 1, on a contract that will run through 2028. "I’ve followed her closely over the last few years and have always believed in the level she can reach,” said team boss Frank Schleck. "At Lidl–Trek, our ambition is not only to bring together the best talent, but to create an environment where riders can develop, challenge themselves and reach their full potential. We believe we can give Blanka exactly that."Her versatility, racing instinct and team mentality will make us stronger across the entire calendar. She has already proven her quality on the road and in cyclocross, and we’re especially excited that she’ll pull on the Lidl–Trek jersey very soon for the upcoming CX season. Blanka represents exactly the kind of ambitious, multi-discipline rider we want to build our future around.”As for Vas herself, she was quoted in the announcements from both teams. “This was not an easy decision, but after a number of discussions, we all felt that this was the right time to take a different path,” she said in the SD Worx press release. “I would like to thank everyone at Team SD Worx-Protime for their support, professionalism, dedication and friendship over the past 5.5 years. It is now time for a new chapter in my career.”Soon after, in Lidl-Trek’s press release, she added: “I have very good feelings about it and can’t wait to get to know everyone in the team. I am super excited. I’m mostly looking forward to the new environment, the new challenges and everything I can learn. I’m excited to start this new chapter, get to know everyone and see what we can achieve together as a team.“I hope I can keep improving and become a stronger rider. I’d also like to get some experience in a leadership role at some races and see how I can handle that. I think it would be a good opportunity for me to learn and grow.”Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: 'My body can't take it anymore' – Mattias Skjelmose withdraws from World Championships after Vuelta a España suffering
item.author: Patrick Fletcher
item.content:encoded: Mattias Skjelmose, described by the national coach Michal Mørkøv as Denmark's best hope for the World Championships, has withdrawn from the event after suffering through the final days of the Vuelta a España. Skjelmose, who finished sixth in the Tour de France and is a previous winner of hilly Classics such as Amstel Gold Race, was set to lead the line for Denmark in the Montréal Worlds road race on September 27 alongside Mads Pedersen. However, having started the final week of the Vuelta in 7th place overall, the 25-year-old slipped to 13th by the end of the race, and informed Mørkøv of his decision to pull out of Worlds on Sunday, ahead of the Vuelta's final stage. "I told Michael that I have to cancel because my body can't take it anymore," Skjelmose told the Danish broadcaster . "I love being part of the national team and have had some of the best experiences of my career there. But I also don't think it's fair to take a position from another Dane who is really doing well."Skjelmose will be replaced in Denmark's line-up by Anton Charmig, who just before Skjelmose's decision had put in an eye-catching ride to third place at the Grand Prix de Québec. "You answer quickly when you see that Michael Mørkøv is on the phone," the Uno-X rider told TV2. "It was a fantastic race on Friday. It was the best I've ever ridden, so my form is better than ever."The loss of Skjelmose is a huge blow for Denmark, even if his declining form was already ominous. The Lidl-Trek rider has had a strong season and has proven in the past that he can win hilly one-day races, most notably in 2024 when he beat Tadej Pogačar to win Amstel Gold Race – one of the current world champion's very rare recent defeats. Skjelmose had been billed as Denmark's leader alongside Mads Pedersen, who faces question marks over how he'll deal with the elevation gain on the Montréal course, as well as over his own form after he had to make an early exit from the Vuelta. "It's a huge disappointment, because there's no doubt that in my eyes Mattias was our biggest chance for a world champion on that route in Montreal," Mørkøv told TV2. "It's actually to be expected, at least from where I've seen Mattias the last few days. It hasn't looked very promising. [Anton] rode absolutely fantastically in Québec last Friday. So it's convenient and well-deserved that we can get such a strong replacement for Mattias."Alongside Pedersen and Charmig, the other riders in Denmark's Worlds squad are: Michael Valgren, Mikkel Bjerg, Kasper Asgreen, Søren Kragh Andersen, Andreas Kron, and Mikkel Honoré.

item.title: 'Winning would maybe be the next logical step' - Felix Gall cautiously optimistic after second 2026 Grand Tour podium finish at Vuelta a España
item.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
item.content:encoded: Six days before the Vuelta a España finished, Felix Gall was asked by Spanish newspaper MARCA to draw a final GC podium on a piece of paper with the names of who would occupy each position, and his answer was spot on: first Enric Mas, second Primož Roglič and third Gall himself.The Austrian's confidence that he could hold third was perhaps ambitious given Richard Carapaz, running fourth, was making some hugely unpredictable attacks that at times seemed close to blowing the entire race apart. But in fact, just as Gall had managed to already finish as 'first of the mortals' behind an unstoppable Jonas Vingegaard (Visma-Lease a Bike) in the Giro d'Italia, his consistent racing for a second Grand Tour in 2026 netted him another top GC Grand Tour result in the same season.Whilst the last rider to complete the Giro and Vuelta on the podium without winning either was Miguel Ángel 'Superman' López back in 2018, third in both races, Gall's next logical objective, he said in his post-race press conference, would be to go for a Grand Tour win. However, the 28-year-old also issued a note of caution about his chances of that actually happening, pointing out that he had already raised the bar considerably in terms of overall performances in Grand Tours in 2026. As he put it, "that's a huge step."One year ago, in the winter, the goal was to be on the podium of a Grand Tour and that already seemed pretty ambitious," Gall told reporters. "We thought it could be possible but only if everything went really well.""Now this year I once again made a step, so winning a Grand Tour would maybe be the next logical one to do, but it's a huge step and you can't force that."Enric was on the podium four times before winning a first Grand Tour so it takes a while maybe to be in this position one day."But for sure, after this season I invested a lot, I pushed myself harder than I did in previous years and maybe I can progress a little more in the next years."You can't force it, though. I can only do my best season and see what that is going to be."Victory in the Vuelta a Burgos showed in August that Gall was more than prepared for the challenge of doing for a second Grand Tour in a single year at the Vuelta a España, but even in Monaco, he had made it clear that a podium in Spain was the target.That was only logical given a certain Tadej Pogačar was in control of the race at the time, and while Gall did manage to open up an advantage on Enric Mas at Valdelinares on stage 7, the day before he had been on the backfoot, losing much more time when Mas pulled away over the Puerto de el Bartolo. Once Pogačar had been forced to abandon, it was a similar scenario with Mas being superior in general on the climbs, whilst Roglič, if not so powerful on the sumit finishes, was able to use his time trialling skills to keep the Austrian out of second place overall."Enric was super strong for the whole three weeks, he didn't show any weakness, also as a team they did a great job defending the jersey," Gall said. "And Primož was also a super strong rider, so that's the right order on the podium for sure. I did my best, but time trialling is not my strong suit, so I lost a bit of time there."But I'm happy with my performance on the last stages, and we can have no regrets as a team."At the end of the race, there were only five guys here for us, maybe that made a bit of a difference. But I'm proud of how they did and I'm pleased I didn't make any big mistakes, either."The critical last weekend did see Gall briefly drop Mas on the Collado del Alguacil, the hardest single climb of the entire Vuelta. But whilst encouraging, it didn't really make a big difference overall, as Mas knew he had won overall by that point, and the time gaps were such that Gall didn't constitute a threat to him, only to Roglič - and even that was going to need a major collapse by the Slovenian, which didn't happen."My goal here was to be on the podium before the race and that didn't change," Gall concluded. "Yesterday [Saturday] with Richie [Carapaz] constantly attacking, I was just focussed on him and defending, I didn't want to risk losing it. "I have no regrets, Enric was for sure the strongest throughout and I'm not sure what I could have done differently [to get a better placing.]After his third place in Granada, Gall will now head to the World Championships, where he will be able, like Mas and Roglič to make the most of his Vuelta-hardened condition to perhaps make some kind of outsider challenge.However, in either case, as Gall said by way of conclusion, having finished fifth in the Tour de France in 2025, the next big aim for 2026 was to take a Grand Tour podium. So to do so not once, but twice, already gives him a sense that his season has been a huge success."If you had told me one year ago, I'd get two Grand Tour podiums in 2026, I'd have found that hard to believe," he said before ending his press conference. "So I can only be very happy with this season." item.title: Spanish GP organisers promise Madring track changes following F1 criticism
The World Championships moments we will always remember – Iconic victories, crushing heartbreaks, dramatic twists, and more
item.author: Matilda Price
item.content:encoded: The 2026 Road World Championships are nearly upon us, and before we crown another round of world champions and rainbow jerseys, the team has been reflecting on the Worlds moments we just can't get out of our heads.From surprise winners to shocking twists, there have been innumerable unforgettable moments at the World Championships over the decades. Rainbow jersey races are always something, where absolutely anything can – and will – happen, and just because the winner is always the strongest rider on the day, that doesn't mean that these races are ever predictable or straightforward. Far from it, in fact.Between the team, we've been to countless World Championships over the years, be it reporting as journalists or watching as fans, and we all have moments that we hold dear, for different reasons – some moments are emotional, some are exhilarating, and some are just cold and wet. Ranging from the 1980s to the 2020s, here are our picks for some of our most memorable World Championships moments over the year. Lizzie Deignan's rainbow jersey sprint in RichmondOnly a year or two into watching cycling properly, I didn't really know much about the World Championships going into 2015, except that they were – obviously – really important. I had no idea of Team GB's history at Worlds, Project Cavendish from 2010, Nicole Cooke's victory in 2009, nothing. I just knew I was looking out for GB jerseys, and I wanted Lizzie Deignan to win.I don't remember the full race in all that much detail, but the final few hundred metres are seared into my memory as one of the most thrilling and exciting races I'd seen at that moment in time. Deignan came around the sprinting orange figure of Anna van der Breggen early, possibly too early, and when the camera switched to the head-on angle, it felt like the win would never come. The seconds felt like hours, honestly, so hard was I willing Lizzie to hold Anna off, and even when they crossed the line you couldn't quite tell who had won. But then, Lizzie had her hand clasped over her mouth in a now-iconic image of shock and disbelief at the fact she had just won world champion, and I was as thrilled and elated as she was. My favourite rider had just pulled off a huge win in a nailbiting finish, and got to pull on the rainbow jersey in Richmond that afternoon. It was a dream come true for her, and honestly, a bit of a dream for me too.Cadel Evans' attempted defence at his home 2010 World ChampionshipsAt that time, I wasn't working in cycling but was just an avid fan who had actually been drawn into road cycling via an interest in the off-road disciplines, with Evans' crossover from mountain biking to the road no small contributor to that process. That made a pilgrimage roadside to Geelong – only a couple of hours away from home – to watch the racing unfold a no-brainer. Our extended family group, including my young children and nephews, trekked up Challambra Crescent, with the help of prams and piggy backs, so we could absorb the excitement of the race as it unfolded on that short but sharp climb that delivered a pivotal point on the finishing circuit. As a result we got to witness an incredibly spirited defense by Evans, with the roaring crowd delivering an electric atmosphere as he once again gritted his teeth and set off in pursuit of a charging Philippe Gilbert on the ascent near the end of the race. It was not a moment that resulted in a win, for either, but it is still is happily burnt into the memory as one of my favourite experiences as a spectator. The sheer scale and intensity of that collective excitement and anticipation is something rarely associated with a sport that usually lives in the shadows in Australia and it helped feed and consolidate a growing passion for the sport. So, regardless of the outcome of the racing in Montréal, now I'm hoping that the Canadians roadside as Vallieres launches her defence get to experience their own World Championships moment that will end up seared into memory. Abraham Olano punctures but hangs on for 1995 titleHosted at the highest ever altitude (2,500 metres above sea level) and mostly in a torrential rain storm, the 1995 World Championships men's road race in Colombia was one of the hardest in history, with just 20 finishers. The crunch moment came when Abraham Olano jumped away late on for Spain, whilst Miguel Indurain, clearly the strongest rider present, and Fernando Escartin kept the opposition under control behind. However, there was a colossal twist in the tail when Olano punctured late on and, not having enough of a margin to stop, continued on a totally deflated back wheel for nearly two kilometres. He made it to the finish line upright, but it was touch and go all the way.Olano's victory, despite being so hard-earned, sparked uproar in Spain because it was considered by many non-cycling fans that Indurain, a five-time Tour de France winner and the big favourite for Spain, should have gone for the win. But in fact the Spanish national squad pulled off a strategic masterpiece, and the way Indurain punched the air to celebrate Olano's win when he crossed the line for silver amply confirmed Indurain's delight at a teammate's victory.Mathieu van der Poel's crash in Glasgow 2023The World Championships road race in Glasgow was the last race I went to before starting my job with, still viewing it through the eyes of a fan instead of a journalist. Setting up in the early morning on Montrose Street in Glasgow with my Dad, we watched the opening half of the race hunched over my phone, power banks and sustenance for the day at the ready, before enjoying 10 laps of criterium racing heaven on one of the hardest parts of the course. As the top riders in the world came to the fore, nothing stuck with me as much as the moment when eventual winner Mathieu van der Poel crashed, having dropped Tadej Pogačar, Wout van Aert, and Mads Pedersen to go solo. We'd been standing on the roadside between a set of Belgian fans and Danish fans, who both cheered when the Dutchman came down in the rain, having almost lost faith when their respective heroes were unable to match him.Watching this all unfold on a time lag, 5G stream, meant that when Van der Poel came around the corner at the foot of Montrose Street, skinsuit ripped, shoe broken, and met by a roar of the Scottish faithful, many were expecting the chasers to be right on his tail. But the expectation soon turned to a collective groan around us as the Belgian's realised the Dutchman had enough in the bank to still win solo, capturing the rainbow jersey after an epic race that I won't forget being there to see.A 19-year-old Marianne Vos wins in SalzburgIt is so, so, so hard to choose one World Championships victory because so many have evoked emotion, sparked inspiration, and led to endless storytelling during my career in sports journalism. I've been lucky enough to watch and report in person on a handful of road World Championships from Hamilton in 2003, Salzburg in 2006, Richmond in 2015, Innsbruck in 2018, Yorkshire in 2019, and Kigali in 2025.However, I have to choose 2006 because it was an important year for women's pro racing, marking the start of Marianne Vos' elite road racing career with her victory at the Salzburg World Championships, where she beat Trixi Worrack and Nicole Cooke.Still a teenager, she had already won the elite cyclo-cross world title earlier that year, and it was clear she was the future of the sport. Her win in Salzburg ignited a career that embodied nearly everything cycling has to offer.And so, 14 multi-discipline World Championship titles later, Vos has taken us all on a two-decade-long journey that showcases herself as an extraordinary athlete, fierce competitor, and adaptable and humble leader, and figurehead for progress and change, who is now widely regarded as the greatest cyclist of all time.The second of Julian Alaphilippe's two winsJulian Alaphilippe’s second World Championship victory is my most memorable Worlds moment. When I think of Alaphilippe’s win back in 2021, the word that springs to mind is 'brave'. The Frenchman produced a fearless title defence in Leuven. Racing with number 1 on his back, his multiple searing attacks had fans on the edge of their seats and resulted in a popular solo victory.Alaphilippe began attacking with just under 50 kilometres to go and simply refused to admit defeat. In the final kilometres, the gap to the chasers hung in the balance for a while, a mere handful of seconds, before the elastic finally snapped and the gap went out. More victories followed, but apart from a Giro stage in 2024, it was Alaphilippe’s last major win. His efforts represented something of a changing of the guard; it was a win for cotton cycling socks, two-piece handlebars and stems, and he-who-dares, attacking panache. Lotte Kopecky's super win at the Super WorldsLotte Kopecky’s first World Championships win in the 2023 Glasgow 'Super Worlds’ was peak Kopecky. In her second season with SD Worx, she was winning regularly for the first time in her career, a second Tour of Flanders and five days in the Tour de France Femmes yellow jersey after winning the opening stage the highlights. She eventually finished second overall in France and there was plenty more success.With rainbow jerseys in the Elimination and Points races already neatly packed away, confidence was high when she took the start at Loch Lomond, and she rode like the rider she was: the best in the world. Already at the front of the race, her race winning move on the fearsomely steep Montrose Street was devastating.I was working elsewhere in the sport, a company outing placing me on the barrier on the finish line, and I’ll never forget the emotion from Kopecky and the crowd. It was overwhelming.Nils Eekhoff and the world title that never wasThere was something in the air at the 2019 Worlds in Yorkshire. It was pure drama from start to finish. We had Johan Price-Pejtersen splashing into a puddle of water so deep it fully submerged him. We had a Colombian junior crying at the roadside after mechanical support drove past him. We had Rohan Dennis coming back after his Tour de France walk-out and winning the TT on a blacked-out bike. We had Annemiek van Vleuten deciding to do basically the whole road race solo. And we had Mathieu van der Poel bonking out of a winning hand. But what sticks out most vividly in my mind is Nils Eekhoff and the world title that never was. The Dutchman thought he’d won the U23 road race, only to be later informed that he was being disqualified for drafting hours earlier. Reporting on this was chaos, as we tried to make sense of what was happening. The podium ceremony was delayed, UCI officials criss-crossed the mixed zone, and Tom Pidcock, who finished fourth, was still hanging around for reasons that eventually became clear. I remember Pidcock going over to remonstrate with an angry Dutch fan who was looking for someone to blame and was shouting ‘F*** you, Pidcock!’. I then skipped the press conference and ran to the Dutch team’s hotel, where the press officer agreed to bring Eekhoff down for an interview with myself and two other journalists. He sat there in tears and quietly explained the confusion and devastation he was feeling.I don’t want this whole entry to sound like I enjoy watching young people cry, but it was quite something to witness that raw unfiltered emotion from a metre away, and to try and convey it. It was a good get journalistically, and it was a reminder of just how much the Worlds mean and how much they matter to these youngsters who dream of becoming professional cyclists.Greg LeMond brings the jersey home to the US in 1989Greg LeMond's 1989 World Championships victory should never have happened. He had been shot two years earlier, and was still carrying around lead pellets in his body even as he defeated Laurent Fignon in the final time trial to win the Tour de France by eight seconds. It was one of the most incredible comebacks in sporting history, and one that pushed cycling technology into the future.In a stormy Worlds road race in Chambéry, Fignon looked as if he'd exact revenge, darting away on the final climb - but LeMond waited and then surged up to the Frenchman, who attacked again, only for LeMond to shut it down. The race came down to a sprint LeMond should never have won against the likes of Sean Kelly, but LeMond started the sprint from the front and with a much bigger gear, the American held everyone off to celebrate his second rainbow jersey. Again, his choice of equipment - the first carbon fibre frame and a huge gear - along with his talent proved to be the winning element.An honorable mention: Matej Mohoric's no-brakes descent in Florence to win the U23 road race.The 2019 finish line freezeMy first World Championships for and a home Worlds no less, I was in Harrogate on tech duty, and I headed to the finish line as the elite men's road race came to a close. I wasn't the only one surprised by Mads Pedersen's win, but impressive as that was, it's not what sticks in my mind. The memorable moment for me was seeing some of the world's best athletes absolutely cracked by the British weather; dozens of riders with barely any body fat, shivering at the roadside, no doubt questioning their career choice. The above photo of Matteo Trentin's thousand-yard stare lives in my mind – and my camera roll – rent free. As does the look of helplessness as Chad Haga looked to me – or anyone – for assistance as his frozen fingers couldn't operate the zipper on his wet-through rain jacket.That race has gone down as one of the most brutal World Champs in recent history, and I got to witness it first-hand.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews.
